title: Anna's Weekend by the Sea
paragraphs: Anna is twenty-five years old.
She lives in a small flat in a big city and works in an office.
Her job is busy, and she is often tired.
One Friday evening, her friend Kate called her.
"Let's go to the sea this weekend!" Kate said.
"I've already booked a room in a hotel near the beach."
Anna smiled.
"That's a wonderful idea!"
On Saturday morning, Anna got up early.
She packed her suitcase: a T-shirt, shorts, a sweater, sunglasses and a towel.
She had a quick breakfast, toast with butter and a cup of coffee, and went to the station.
At the station, there was a long queue for tickets.
Anna waited for twenty minutes and bought a return ticket.
Then a woman at the information desk said, "The train is late."
Anna was worried, but Kate was calm.
"Never mind," she said.
"We can have a coffee and chat."
The journey took three hours.
Through the window, Anna saw fields, forests, small villages and a river.
When they arrived, the weather was warm and sunny.
The hotel was clean and comfortable, and from their balcony they had a beautiful view of the sea.
In the afternoon, the friends went to the beach.
They swam in the sea, lay on the sand and talked about their plans for the future.
Kate wants to travel abroad next year.
Anna hopes to find a new job with a better salary.
In the evening, they had dinner at a local restaurant.
The waiter was very friendly and polite.
Anna ordered fish with rice and a salad, and Kate chose a delicious seafood soup.
For dessert, they both had ice cream.
After dinner, they walked back to the hotel.
Suddenly Anna stopped.
"Oh no!
Where is my wallet?"
She looked in her bag and in her pockets, but they were empty.
Anna felt terrible.
Her money, her credit card and her driving licence were all in that wallet.
Then they heard someone shout.
It was the waiter!
He was running after them with the wallet in his hand.
"You forgot this on the table," he said.
Anna was surprised and very happy.
"Thank you so much!
You're very kind," she said.
On Sunday, it started to rain, so the friends visited a museum and bought some souvenirs.
In the evening, they took the train home.
"It was a short holiday, but I feel much better now," Anna said.
"Let's do it again soon!"

title: Tom's First Day at Work
paragraphs: Tom is twenty-three.
Last month he finished university, and after many interviews he finally found a job.
He is going to work as a designer at a small company in the city centre.
On Monday morning, Tom woke up at six o'clock.
He was a little worried, so he couldn't eat much breakfast.
He put on his new shirt and his best shoes, took his bag and left the flat early.
He didn't want to be late on his first day.
The office was on the fifth floor of a modern building.
At reception, a friendly woman smiled at him.
"Good morning!
You must be Tom.
Welcome to the company!"
She gave him a card with his name on it and took him upstairs in the lift.
His boss, Mrs Green, was waiting for him.
She was about fifty, with short grey hair and kind eyes.
"Nice to meet you, Tom," she said.
"Let me introduce you to the team."
Tom met his new colleagues: Lisa, a quiet and polite girl who works with computers; Mark, a funny man who always tells jokes; and Sam, an engineer from Canada.
Then Mrs Green showed him his desk.
It was next to a big window with a wonderful view of the river.
On the desk there was a new laptop, a notebook and a cup with the name of the company on it.
The morning was busy.
Tom had to read a lot of information, check his email and learn the rules of the office.
At first he felt confused, but his colleagues were very helpful.
When he didn't understand something, Lisa explained it to him slowly.
At one o'clock, everyone went to a small café near the office for lunch.
Tom ordered a chicken sandwich and an orange juice.
Mark talked about his hobby: he plays the guitar in a band at the weekend.
Sam told funny stories about his life in Canada.
Tom laughed a lot and started to feel more relaxed.
In the afternoon, Mrs Green gave Tom his first project.
He had to design a new website for a customer.
"Take your time," she said.
"You don't have to finish it today."
Tom worked hard and forgot about the time.
When he looked at the clock, it was already half past five.
Before he went home, Mrs Green stopped at his desk.
She looked at his work and said, "That's a good start, Tom.
I think you'll be very successful here."
On the bus home, Tom called his mother.
"How was your first day?" she asked.
"Tiring, but great," Tom answered.
"I think I'm going to enjoy this job."

title: At the Doctor's
paragraphs: Maria is a student.
She studies biology at university and works part-time in a bookshop.
Last week she didn't feel well.
On Monday she had a headache, and on Tuesday she started to cough.
She thought it was just a cold, so she didn't do anything about it.
On Wednesday morning, she woke up with a sore throat and a high temperature.
Her whole body hurt, and she felt very tired.
She couldn't go to her lessons, so she called the bookshop and told her boss that she was ill.
"Stay at home and rest," he said.
"Your health is more important."
Her flatmate, Anna, was worried.
"You look terrible," she said.
"You should see a doctor."
Maria didn't want to go, but Anna called the clinic and booked an appointment for eleven o'clock.
The clinic was not far, but Maria felt too weak to walk, so they took a taxi.
In the waiting room there were a lot of people: an old man, a mother with a crying baby and a young man with a broken arm.
They waited for forty minutes.
Finally, a nurse called Maria's name.
The doctor was a tall man with glasses.
"What's wrong?" he asked.
Maria told him about her headache, her cough and her sore throat.
The doctor checked her temperature.
It was thirty-nine degrees.
Then he looked at her throat and listened to her heart.
"You've got the flu," he said.
"It's not dangerous, but you must stay in bed for a few days.
Drink a lot of water and hot tea with honey and lemon."
He wrote the name of some medicine on a piece of paper.
"Take one pill three times a day, after meals.
And don't go to work or university until you feel better."
On the way home, they stopped at a pharmacy and bought the medicine.
Anna also went to the supermarket and bought fruit, vegetables and a chicken.
In the evening she cooked a big pan of chicken soup.
"My grandmother always made this soup when I was ill," she said.
"It's the best medicine!"
For the next three days, Maria slept a lot, read a novel and watched films on her laptop.
She took her pills and drank lots of tea.
Her friends sent her messages and funny videos.
By Sunday her temperature was normal, and she felt much better.
On Monday she went back to university.
"Thank you for looking after me," she said to Anna.
"You're a wonderful friend."
Anna smiled.
"No problem.
But next time, go to the doctor earlier!"

title: The New Flat
paragraphs: Last spring, Peter and his wife Emma decided to move.
Their old flat was small and dark, and it was in a noisy street near the motorway.
They wanted a bigger, quieter place with a garden for their dog, Max.
For two months they looked for a new home.
They visited a lot of flats and houses, but some were too expensive, some were too far from the city centre, and some were dirty and old.
Emma was almost ready to give up.
Then one day Peter found a flat on the internet: two bedrooms on the ground floor, with a small garden, in a quiet neighbourhood near a park.
The rent wasn't cheap, but it was OK for them.
They met the landlord, an elderly man called Mr Brown.
He showed them around.
The living room was large and bright, with big windows.
The kitchen had a new cooker, a fridge, a dishwasher and a washing machine.
Emma loved it at once.
They signed the papers the same day.
Moving day was hard work.
Peter's brother came with a big car to help them.
They packed everything into boxes: books, plates, cups, clothes and toys for Max.
The heaviest thing was the sofa.
It was too wide for the door, so they had to turn it on its side.
Peter hurt his back a little, but they finally got it inside.
In the evening, the new flat was full of boxes, and everything was a mess.
They were too tired to cook, so they ordered a pizza and ate it on the floor of the living room.
Max ran around the garden happily.
The next day there was a knock at the door.
It was their neighbour, a friendly woman called Mrs Taylor.
She brought them a cake.
"Welcome to the neighbourhood!" she said.
"If you need anything, just ask."
She told them about the local shops, the bus stop and the best place to buy fresh bread.
During the next few weeks, Peter and Emma slowly made the flat their home.
They painted the bedroom walls light green, bought new curtains and a comfortable armchair, and hung pictures on the walls.
Emma planted flowers and tomatoes in the garden.
Peter built a small wooden house for Max.
One warm Saturday in June, they invited their family and friends to a party.
Everyone sat in the garden, ate, talked and laughed until late.
"Your new home is lovely," said Peter's mother.
Peter looked at Emma and smiled.
"Yes," he said.
"It was hard work, but now it's perfect."

title: The Birthday Surprise
paragraphs: Next Friday is Grandma Rose's seventieth birthday.
Her grandchildren, Lucy and Ben, want to do something special for her.
"Let's have a surprise party!" said Lucy.
Ben liked the idea, but they had only one week to prepare everything.
First, they made a plan.
Lucy wrote a list of guests: all the family, Grandma's old friends from work and her neighbours.
Ben sent the invitations by email and text message.
"Please don't tell Grandma," he wrote.
"It's a secret!"
Then they had to choose a place.
Grandma's house was too small for forty people, so they booked a room in a restaurant in the village.
The owner was very kind and gave them a discount.
On Wednesday, Lucy and Ben went to the shopping centre to buy a present.
It was difficult to decide.
"What about a new bag?" asked Ben.
"She already has three," Lucy answered.
They looked at clothes, books and scarves, but nothing seemed right.
Finally, in a small shop, Lucy found a beautiful photo album.
"We can fill it with old family photos," she said.
"Grandma will love it!"
It was quite expensive, so they paid by credit card and shared the cost.
On Thursday evening, they collected old photos from all the family: Grandma as a little girl, at her wedding, and with her children at the beach.
They put the photos in the album and wrote short messages under each one.
On Friday, Ben's job was to keep Grandma busy.
He invited her for a walk in the park and then for a coffee.
At the same time, Lucy and the rest of the family got the restaurant ready.
They hung balloons on the walls and put flowers on every table.
The waiters brought the food: salads, chicken, fish and a huge chocolate cake with seventy candles.
At seven o'clock, Ben's phone rang.
It was Lucy.
"We're ready!" she whispered.
Ben said to Grandma, "Let's have dinner at the restaurant.
I'll pay."
Grandma agreed.
When they walked in, the room was dark.
Suddenly the lights came on, and everyone shouted, "Surprise!
Happy birthday!"
Grandma was so shocked that she couldn't speak.
Then she started to laugh and cry at the same time.
Everyone sang, and Grandma blew out the candles.
When she opened her present and saw the old photos, she had tears in her eyes.
"This is the best birthday of my life," she said.
"Thank you, my dears."
That night, she danced with all her grandchildren until midnight.

title: Lost in Rome
paragraphs: Last summer, Daniel travelled abroad alone for the first time.
He went to Rome for five days.
He was excited, but also a little worried, because he didn't speak Italian.
On the third day, he decided to visit a famous old church on the other side of the city.
In the morning, he left his hotel with a map and his phone.
He wanted to walk, because the weather was lovely and he wanted to see the narrow streets and small squares.
For the first hour, everything was fine.
He stopped at a market and bought some fruit, then he took photos of an ancient building.
But soon the streets became more and more confusing.
They all looked the same.
Daniel looked at his map, but he couldn't find the name of the street.
Then he took out his phone, but the battery was empty!
He forgot to charge it the night before.
Daniel felt afraid.
He was lost in a big foreign city, he didn't know the language, and his phone didn't work.
He walked for another twenty minutes, but he only got more lost.
It was hot, and he was hungry and thirsty.
Finally, he saw a small café on a corner.
An old man was sitting at a table outside, reading a newspaper.
Daniel went up to him.
"Excuse me," he said slowly.
"Do you speak English?
I'm lost."
The man smiled.
"A little," he answered.
"Where do you want to go?"
Daniel showed him the name of the church on the map.
The man laughed.
"Oh, it's very near!
But first, sit down.
You look tired."
He ordered two coffees and a glass of water for Daniel.
They talked for half an hour.
The man's name was Marco.
He was a retired teacher, and his son lived in London.
He told Daniel about the history of the area and gave him the name of a good local restaurant.
Then Marco walked with him to the church.
It was only ten minutes away.
"Here you are," he said.
"Enjoy Rome!"
Daniel thanked him again and again.
The church was amazing, but Daniel decided that the best part of his day was not the sightseeing.
It was the conversation with Marco.
That evening, he had dinner at Marco's restaurant.
The pasta was delicious.
When he got back home, Daniel sent Marco a card.
"Thank you for your help," he wrote.
"Next time I come to Rome, I'll buy the coffee!"
Now, before he goes out in a new city, Daniel always remembers two things: charge your phone, and don't be afraid to ask for help.

title: The Cooking Competition
paragraphs: Sophie loves cooking.
When she was a child, she often helped her father in the kitchen.
Now she is nineteen, and her friends say that her food is better than in any restaurant.
One day, she saw a sign at her college: "Cooking Competition!
Cook a meal for three people in one hour.
First prize: a weekend in Paris."
Sophie decided to enter.
She filled in the form and sent it the same day.
For the next two weeks, she practised every evening.
She wanted to cook something simple but special: fish with lemon, fried potatoes and a fresh salad, and for dessert, a chocolate cake with strawberries.
Her family tasted everything.
"Too salty," said her brother one day.
"Not sweet enough," said her mother the next day.
Sophie changed the recipe again and again until it was perfect.
On the day of the competition, the college hall was full of people.
There were ten students and three judges: a famous cook, a food journalist and the head of the college.
Each student had a table with a cooker, an oven, pans, bowls and knives.
"You have one hour," said the famous cook.
"Start now!"
Sophie worked quickly.
She washed the vegetables, cut the potatoes and started to fry them.
Then she mixed the flour, sugar, eggs and butter for the cake and put it in the oven.
Everything was going well.
But after forty minutes, she opened the oven and saw that the cake was burning!
She felt terrible.
There was no time to bake a new one.
Sophie stayed calm.
She looked around her table.
She had strawberries, chocolate and some biscuits.
Quickly, she broke the biscuits into pieces and put them in glasses, then added the strawberries and melted chocolate on top.
It looked lovely.
When the hour finished, the judges tasted every dish.
They didn't say anything.
They only wrote notes.
Sophie's hands were shaking.
Finally, the famous cook stood up.
"Third place goes to Tom.
Second place goes to Anna.
And the winner is...
Sophie!"
Everyone clapped.
"Your fish was excellent," he said, "but the dessert was the best.
It's a new idea, and it's very tasty.
What do you call it?"
Sophie laughed.
"I call it 'The Mistake'!
My cake burned, so I made something different."
A week later, Sophie and her father went to Paris.
They visited markets, bakeries and restaurants and tasted lots of new dishes.
"Now I have so many new ideas," Sophie said.
"Next year, I want to win again!"

title: A Rainy Weekend
paragraphs: Jack had big plans for the weekend.
He wanted to go hiking in the hills with his friends and have a picnic by the lake.
But on Saturday morning, he looked out of the window and saw grey clouds and heavy rain.
The weather forecast said: "Rain all weekend, with strong wind and a storm in the afternoon."
"Oh no," Jack said.
He called his friends, and they cancelled the trip.
Jack lay on the sofa and felt bored.
What could he do at home for two whole days?
First, he turned on the TV, but there was nothing interesting on.
Then he played a computer game for an hour, but it wasn't fun alone.
He looked at his phone, read some news and checked social media.
Everybody's photos looked sunny and happy, but they were all from last summer.
Then his little sister Mia came into the room.
She was eight.
"I'm bored too," she said.
"Let's do something together!"
"Like what?" Jack asked.
"Let's make a film!" Mia said.
Jack laughed, but then he thought it was a good idea.
They found an old camera in a drawer.
Mia wrote a short story about a brave cat that lived on an island and looked for gold.
Jack held the camera, and Mia was the actor.
Their real cat, Snowy, was the star, but she didn't want to work.
She just wanted to sleep!
They used blankets, pillows and boxes to build a ship in the living room.
Mia's toys were the bad men on the island.
They put on funny hats and old clothes from the wardrobe.
During the storm in the afternoon, they recorded the sound of the thunder and the wind for their film.
On Sunday, they finished the film on Jack's laptop.
They added music and wrote the title: "Captain Snowy and the Secret Island".
It was only ten minutes long, but it took the whole day.
In the evening, their parents came home.
Mia and Jack made popcorn, turned off the lights and showed them the film.
Their parents laughed so much that their mother cried.
"This is wonderful!" said their father.
"You should put it online."
Jack uploaded the video, and by Monday, five hundred people had watched it.
His friends sent him messages: "Your film is so funny!
Can we be in the next one?"
Jack smiled.
He didn't go hiking, but it was one of the best weekends of the year.
"Sometimes," he thought, "rain is not so bad."

title: The Big Match
paragraphs: Leo is fifteen and plays football for his school team.
He practises three times a week after lessons, and on Saturdays the team plays matches against other schools.
This year, his team did very well, and now they were in the final of the city competition.
The final was on Saturday at the city stadium.
All week, Leo couldn't think about anything else.
In class, he didn't listen to the teacher, and at night he dreamed about scoring goals.
On Friday, the coach, Mr Wilson, called the team together.
"Tomorrow will be difficult," he said.
"The other team is strong and fast.
But if you work together as a team, you can win.
Go to bed early, eat a good breakfast and don't be late."
On Saturday, the stadium was full.
Leo's parents and his little brother sat in the crowd with a big sign: "GO, LEO!"
When the players came out, everybody shouted and clapped.
Leo's legs felt heavy.
The first half was terrible for Leo's team.
After ten minutes, the other team scored a goal.
Then, just before half-time, they scored again.
In the break, the players were sad and angry.
Some of them shouted at each other.
Mr Wilson stayed calm.
"Listen," he said.
"Shouting doesn't help.
Two goals is not the end of the world.
Stop playing alone and pass the ball.
Believe in yourselves."
In the second half, the team played much better.
They passed the ball and helped each other.
After sixty minutes, Leo's best friend Omar scored.
The crowd went crazy.
Ten minutes later, Leo kicked the ball from the corner, and Omar hit it with his head.
Two all!
The last minutes were very exciting.
Everyone in the stadium was standing.
Then, in the ninetieth minute, Leo got the ball.
He ran past one player, then another.
He was alone in front of the goal.
He kicked, and the ball flew into the net!
A few seconds later, the game was over.
Leo's team won three to two.
The players jumped and hugged each other, and some of them cried with happiness.
Leo's parents ran onto the field, and his little brother jumped into his arms.
Mr Wilson shook Leo's hand.
"Well done," he said.
"But remember, you didn't win because of one goal.
You won because you didn't give up."
That evening, the whole team had pizza at a local restaurant.
They looked at the cup on the table and laughed about the terrible first half.
Leo knew that he would remember this day for the rest of his life.

title: The Storm in the Mountains
paragraphs: Every summer, the Miller family goes on holiday together.
Usually they stay in a hotel by the sea, but this year sixteen-year-old Emily had a different idea.
"Let's go camping in the mountains," she said.
"No internet, no TV, just nature."
Her father liked the idea at once.
Her mother was not so sure, and her twelve-year-old brother Josh was angry.
"No Wi-Fi for a whole week?
That's terrible!"
But in the end, Emily won.
In July, they packed the car with a tent, warm sweaters, boots, food, a small cooker and a box of medicine.
They drove for six hours to a national park in the north.
The road went higher and higher, past lakes, forests and waterfalls.
Even Josh put his phone away and looked out of the window.
"Wow," he said quietly.
"It's beautiful."
The campsite was next to a clear blue lake.
There were only a few other tents, and the air was fresh and cool.
Their father and Josh put up the tent, while Emily and her mother collected wood for a fire.
In the evening, they cooked sausages and potatoes on the fire and watched the sun go down behind the mountains.
When it got dark, they saw thousands of stars.
In the city, you can never see so many.
The first few days were wonderful.
They went hiking along forest paths, swam in the cold lake and had picnics on the hills.
Their father taught Josh how to fish, and on the third day Josh caught a big fish.
He was so proud that he took twenty photos of it, with his phone, of course!
Emily drew pictures of flowers and birds in her notebook, and their mother read books in the sunshine.
Nobody missed the internet.
Well, almost nobody.
On the fifth day, they decided to climb to the top of the highest mountain in the park.
A man who worked in the park gave them some advice.
"The weather can change very quickly up there," he said.
"Take warm clothes and rain jackets, and come back before three o'clock."
They started early in the morning.
The path was narrow and difficult, and they had to stop often to rest.
But the views were amazing.
After four hours, they finally reached the top.
They could see for many kilometres in every direction: green valleys, dark forests and lakes that looked like small mirrors.
They took photos, ate their sandwiches and felt very happy.
But then Emily saw something.
In the west, the sky was getting dark.
Big black clouds were moving towards them very fast.
"Dad," she said, "I think a storm is coming."
They started down the mountain quickly, but after twenty minutes the storm arrived.
First the wind became very strong, then heavy rain started to fall.
There was thunder and lightning all around them.
The path turned into a river of water, and it was difficult to see anything.
Josh fell and hurt his knee.
He sat on a rock and started to cry.
Their father stayed calm.
"We can't continue in this weather," he said.
"It's too dangerous.
We need to find somewhere safe."
Then Emily remembered something.
On the way up, she saw a small wooden house next to the path.
"There's a little house near here!" she shouted.
"Follow me!"
Five minutes later, they found it.
It was old and empty, but it was dry inside.
They took off their wet jackets and sat close together.
Their mother looked at Josh's knee.
It wasn't broken, but it was very sore.
She washed it with water from her bottle and put some medicine on it.
They waited in the little house for two hours.
They were cold and tired, but nobody complained.
They ate the rest of their chocolate and told funny stories.
Josh even laughed when their father sang terrible old songs to make everyone feel better.
At last, the storm stopped.
The sun came out, and there was a huge rainbow over the valley.
Slowly and carefully, they walked down to the campsite.
Josh's knee hurt, but he walked all the way without crying.
That night, they sat by the fire again.
Everyone was very quiet.
"You know," Josh said finally, "today was scary.
But it was also the best adventure of my life.
I'm glad we didn't stay in a hotel."
Emily smiled.
"So you don't miss the Wi-Fi?"
Josh thought for a moment.
"Well... maybe a little," he said.
Everyone laughed.
The next year, the Millers went camping again.
And this time, Josh was the first to say, "Let's go to the mountains!"

title: The Job Interview
paragraphs: Sara was twenty-seven, and for three years she had worked in a busy shop in the town centre.
She liked her colleagues, but the job was boring and the pay was low.
In the evenings she studied marketing online.
She had always dreamed of working in an office with creative people, where her ideas were important.
One Monday morning, she was drinking coffee in the kitchen when her phone rang.
It was a woman called Mrs Taylor from a travel company.
"We have read your application," she said.
"We would like to invite you to an interview on Friday at ten o'clock."
Sara could hardly believe it.
She had sent more than twenty applications, and this was the first answer.
"Thank you so much," Sara said.
"I'll be there."
When she put the phone down, she jumped up and down in the kitchen.
Then she suddenly stopped.
She had never had a real job interview before.
What would they ask?
What should she wear?
What if she said something stupid?
That evening she called her older brother, Daniel.
He worked in a bank and had been to many interviews.
"Don't worry," he told her.
"Prepare well and be yourself.
If you know a lot about the company, they will see that you are interested."
He advised her to read the company's website and to think about her strengths and weaknesses.
For the next four days, Sara prepared every evening after work.
She read everything about the company.
She learned that it was started fifteen years ago by two friends, and that it organised trips for families and young people.
She wrote down possible questions and practised her answers in front of the mirror.
Her flatmate, Lucy, pretended to be the manager.
"Why do you want this job?"
Lucy asked in a deep, serious voice, and they both laughed.
On Thursday night, Sara couldn't sleep.
She kept thinking about the interview.
At two o'clock in the morning she was still awake, looking at the ceiling.
She finally fell asleep at four, and she forgot to set her alarm.
When she woke up, it was already half past eight.
"Oh no!" she shouted.
She jumped out of bed, put on the dark blue dress she had chosen the day before and ran out of the flat without breakfast.
The bus was full and slow because of the traffic.
Sara looked at her watch every minute.
Her heart was beating fast.
She arrived at the office at five to ten, out of breath, but on time.
The receptionist asked her to wait.
Sara sat down and tried to breathe slowly.
Then she noticed something terrible.
In her hurry, she had left her folder at home.
Her CV, her notes and all her answers were on the kitchen table.
At that moment, a tall man with glasses opened the door.
"Sara Collins?
I'm Mr Evans, the manager.
Please come in."
In the room there was also Mrs Taylor, the woman from the phone call.
They both smiled and asked her to sit down.
The first questions were easy.
They asked about her studies and her job in the shop.
Sara answered clearly, and she started to feel a little better.
Then Mr Evans asked, "Tell me, what do you know about our company?"
Sara opened her mouth, but suddenly her mind was empty.
She had read so much, but now she couldn't remember anything.
She said the company was twenty years old.
Mrs Taylor looked at her notes.
"Actually, it's fifteen," she said politely.
Sara felt her face go red.
She wanted to disappear.
For a few seconds nobody spoke.
Sara thought about leaving.
Then she remembered Daniel's words: "Be yourself."
She took a deep breath.
"I'm sorry," she said.
"To be honest, I'm very nervous.
I didn't sleep last night, and this morning I left all my notes at home.
I prepared a lot, but right now my head is a mess.
Can I tell you why I really want this job instead?"
Mr Evans looked surprised, but he nodded.
"Please do."
So Sara told them the truth.
She explained that she had never travelled much as a child because her family didn't have much money.
Her first trip abroad was to Spain when she was nineteen, and it had changed her life.
"I saw that travel isn't only for rich people," she said.
"If I worked here, I would like to help more young people take their first trip.
I have some ideas for cheap student holidays."
She described two of her ideas.
As she spoke, she forgot about being nervous.
Her voice became stronger, and her eyes were shining.
When she finished, Mrs Taylor was smiling.
Mr Evans wrote something in his notebook.
"Thank you, Sara," he said.
"We will call you next week."
On the bus home, Sara felt sure that she had failed.
"I said the wrong year, and I told them I was a mess," she said to Lucy that evening.
"They will never choose me."
Lucy made her a cup of tea and told her to stop worrying.
Six days later, Mrs Taylor called.
Sara's hands were shaking when she answered.
"We have interviewed eight people," Mrs Taylor said.
"Many of them knew every fact about our company.
But you were the only one who was honest with us, and your ideas were excellent.
We would like to offer you the job."
Sara was silent for a moment.
Then she said, "Yes!
Thank you!
Yes!"
A month later, Sara started her new job.
On her first day, Mr Evans showed her to her desk.
"You know," he said, "when you told us the truth, I knew you were the right person.
Anyone can learn facts.
It's much harder to learn honesty."
Sara smiled.
Since that day, she has always kept two things in her bag: a copy of her notes and a second alarm clock.

title: The Neighbour's Secret
paragraphs: When Anna and her ten-year-old son, Ben, moved into the old building on Park Street, everything seemed perfect.
Their flat was small but bright, and the rent was cheap.
The neighbours were quiet, and there was a little garden behind the house where Ben could play football.
Above them lived an old man called Mr Harris.
He was about eighty, tall and thin, with white hair and a grey coat that he wore even in summer.
Anna saw him only on the stairs.
He always said "Good morning" politely, but he never stopped to talk.
Ben thought he looked a bit scary.
About two weeks after they had moved in, Anna woke up in the middle of the night.
She looked at the clock.
It was ten past two.
Somewhere above her, there was a strange noise.
Knock, knock, knock.
Then silence.
Then a long, low sound, like something heavy was being pulled across the floor.
The next night, it happened again.
And the night after that.
Every night, between one and three o'clock, the noises came from Mr Harris's flat.
Sometimes Anna also heard quiet music from an old radio.
At breakfast, Ben looked tired.
"Mum, did you hear it?" he whispered.
"What is he doing up there at night?"
"I don't know," Anna said.
"Maybe he can't sleep."
But Ben had his own ideas.
He had been reading too many detective stories.
"Maybe he's hiding something," he said.
"Or maybe he's building a machine."
Anna laughed, but secretly she was a little worried too.
She decided to ask the other neighbours.
Mrs Patel, who lived on the ground floor, had been in the building for twenty years.
"Oh, Mr Harris is a lovely man," she said.
"But he has been very lonely since his wife died last year.
He used to go out every day.
Now he hardly leaves his flat."
She didn't know anything about the noises.
"I sleep very well," she said with a smile.
"I don't hear anything."
A week later, something else happened.
Anna was coming home from work when she saw Mr Harris on the stairs.
He was carrying a big bag, and it looked very heavy.
Something long and wooden was sticking out of the top.
When he saw Anna, he quickly turned away and went up to his flat.
He closed the door without saying a word.
"You see?" Ben said that evening.
"He's definitely hiding something."
On Saturday, Anna had to go to the post office.
When she came back, she found a small paper package in front of their door.
It had fallen out of somebody's bag.
Inside there were some small pieces of wood, a tube of glue and a piece of paper with drawings.
The drawings showed a little house with windows, stairs and tiny furniture.
At the bottom, someone had written "For the children – St Mary's" in old-fashioned handwriting.
Anna looked at the package for a long time.
Then she said, "Ben, I think we should give this back to Mr Harris."
They went upstairs together and knocked on his door.
For a moment, nothing happened.
Then they heard slow footsteps, and the door opened a little.
Mr Harris looked surprised to see them.
"I think this is yours," Anna said, and she held out the package.
"We found it downstairs."
The old man's face changed.
"Oh, thank you," he said.
"I've been looking for it all morning."
He hesitated for a second.
Then he opened the door wider.
"Would you like to come in?
I can explain the noise.
I'm sure you've heard it."
Anna and Ben stepped inside, and Ben's mouth fell open.
The living room was full of wooden toys.
There were trains, cars, boats and animals on every shelf.
In the middle of the room, on a big table, stood a beautiful doll's house.
It was almost as tall as Ben, with three floors, a red roof and little lights in the windows.
"I used to be a carpenter," Mr Harris said quietly.
"My wife, Mary, was a nurse at St Mary's children's hospital for thirty years.
Every Christmas, I made toys for the children there.
She always said that a toy could make a sick child forget the pain for an hour."
He stopped and looked at a photo on the wall.
It showed a smiling woman in a nurse's uniform.
"After she died, I stopped.
I didn't want to do anything," he continued.
"But a few months ago, I decided that she would be sad if the children didn't get their toys this year.
So I started again.
I can't sleep well at night, so I work then.
I'm sorry about the noise.
I've been moving the doll's house across the room to paint it."
Anna felt tears in her eyes.
"Please don't be sorry," she said.
"We thought you were a mystery.
Now we know you're a hero."
Ben was looking at a small wooden train.
"Mr Harris," he asked shyly, "could you teach me how to make one?"
The old man smiled for the first time.
It was a warm, wide smile.
"If you come on Saturday afternoons, I'll teach you," he said.
"But only in the daytime.
Your mother needs her sleep."
From that week, Ben went upstairs every Saturday.
He learned how to cut wood, use glue and paint small details.
Anna sometimes joined them and brought cake.
Even Mrs Patel came up once to help with the doll's house curtains.
In December, they all went to St Mary's hospital together.
The children's faces lit up when they saw the boxes of toys.
A little girl with a bandage on her arm held the doll's house and refused to let it go.
On the way home, Mr Harris walked slowly between Anna and Ben.
"Mary would be happy," he said.
"This year, I didn't do it alone."
The noises at night have stopped now.
Mr Harris sleeps better, he says.
But on Saturday afternoons, the building is full of the sound of knocking, laughing and an old radio playing music.

title: The Online Shopping Disaster
paragraphs: Kate Wilson hated going to the shops.
The shopping centre was always crowded, the music was too loud and she could never find anything in her size.
So when her best friend, Emma, invited her to her wedding in June, Kate decided to buy everything online.
It was a Sunday evening, three weeks before the wedding.
Kate sat on the sofa with her laptop and a cup of tea.
After an hour of searching, she found the perfect dress.
It was light green, long and elegant, and it was on sale.
She also chose a pair of silver shoes and a small bag.
"Easy," she said to her cat, Pepper.
"Why didn't I always do this?"
She put her name, address and card details into the website and clicked "Buy now".
A message appeared on the screen: "Thank you for your order!
Your parcel will be delivered within five working days."
Kate smiled and went to bed happy.
On Thursday, a parcel arrived.
Kate opened it excitedly.
Inside she found the silver shoes and the bag, but not the dress.
Instead, there was a bright orange T-shirt with a picture of a cartoon duck on it.
It was size XXL.
Kate held it up in front of the mirror.
It was as long as a dress, but it was definitely not a wedding dress.
She looked at the shoes.
At least they were right, she thought.
Then she tried them on.
They were two sizes too small.
She checked her order on the website and saw the problem.
She had chosen size 37, but she had wanted 39.
It was her own mistake.
Kate took a deep breath.
She decided to contact customer service.
On the website there was a chat window.
A message appeared: "Hi, I'm Lily.
How can I help you today?"
Kate explained everything: the orange T-shirt, the missing dress and the shoes that were too small.
She was polite, but she was worried.
"The wedding is in two and a half weeks," she wrote.
"I really need that dress."
"I'm very sorry," Lily answered.
"It seems that your dress was sent to another customer by mistake.
We will send you a new one by express delivery.
It should arrive on Tuesday.
You can also send the shoes back for free, and we'll send you a bigger size."
Kate felt much better.
She packed the T-shirt and the shoes into the box, took it to the post office and sent it back.
"Everything will be fine," she told Pepper.
The cat didn't look so sure.
On Tuesday, Kate stayed at home all day.
She worked on her laptop at the kitchen table and listened for the doorbell.
Nobody came.
At six o'clock in the evening, she got an email.
"Good news!
Your parcel has been delivered."
Kate ran to the door and opened it.
There was nothing there.
She looked behind the plants, under the doormat and even in the rubbish bin.
No parcel.
She went back to the chat.
This time a man called Tom answered.
He checked the information and found a photo that the driver had taken.
It showed a blue door with the number 18 on it.
"That's not my door," Kate wrote.
"I live at number 81!"
Tom said that the driver had probably read the number the wrong way.
He promised to contact the delivery company, but he said it could take a few days.
Kate didn't want to wait a few days.
She put on her coat and walked down Green Street.
Number 18 was at the other end, about ten minutes from her house.
She knocked on the blue door, but nobody answered.
She wrote a short note with her name and phone number, put it through the letterbox and went home.
She felt tired and a little hopeless.
If the dress didn't arrive, she would have to go to the crowded shopping centre after all.
That night, at about ten o'clock, her phone rang.
It was a number she didn't know.
"Hello, is that Kate?" said a friendly voice.
"My name is George.
I live at number 18.
I've just got home from work and found your note.
I think I have something of yours.
A big box with your name on it was in front of my door."
Kate almost dropped the phone.
"Oh, thank you!
I can come and get it now," she said.
"Don't worry, it's late," George said.
"I take my dog for a walk every evening.
I'll bring it to you in ten minutes."
Ten minutes later, there was a knock at the door.
A tall man in his sixties was standing there with a big black dog and the box under his arm.
"Here you are," he said with a smile.
"I hope it's something nice."
Kate opened the box right there on the doorstep.
Inside was the light green dress.
It was exactly the right size.
"It's for my best friend's wedding," she explained.
"You've saved me!"
George laughed.
"My wife and I got married forty years ago," he said.
"She made her own dress.
Things were simpler then, I think."
Kate invited him in for a cup of tea, and they talked for half an hour.
George told her that the same thing had happened to him last year.
His new boots had been delivered to number 81, but the woman who lived there before Kate had never returned them.
"So you see," he said, "the street owes me a pair of boots."
The new shoes, in the right size, arrived on Friday, at the right address.
On the day of the wedding, Kate looked beautiful in her green dress and silver shoes.
Emma loved it.
"Where did you buy it?" she asked.
"Online," Kate said.
"But it's a long story."
The next week, Kate went to a shoe shop in the shopping centre.
She tried on ten pairs of boots and finally bought a warm brown pair in a man's size 44.
Then she walked down Green Street to number 18 and left a box in front of the blue door.
On top, there was a note: "From number 81.
Better late than never.
Thank you, George!"

title: Learning to Drive
paragraphs: Michael was thirty-five years old, and he had never driven a car.
When he was young, he lived in a big city with good buses and trains, so he didn't need one.
Later, he was always too busy.
But last spring, Michael and his wife, Helen, moved to a small village in the countryside.
The nearest supermarket was eight kilometres away, and there was only one bus a day.
"You have to learn to drive," Helen said after their first week in the village.
"I can't take you everywhere."
She was right.
Michael was a bit embarrassed, but he called a local driving school and booked his first lesson.
His instructor was a woman called Mrs Grant.
She was about sixty, with short grey hair and very serious eyes.
She had been a driving instructor for thirty years.
On the first day, she looked at Michael from head to toe.
"Have you ever sat behind the wheel of a car?" she asked.
"Only in video games," Michael answered with a nervous laugh.
Mrs Grant didn't laugh.
"This is not a game," she said.
"A car is a dangerous machine.
If you are careless, people can get hurt.
Do you understand?"
"Yes," Michael said quietly.
He suddenly felt like a schoolboy again.
The first lessons were very difficult.
There were so many things to remember at the same time.
He had to check the mirrors, use the pedals, change gear, turn the wheel and watch the road.
When he tried to start the car, it stopped with a jump.
When he tried again, it made a terrible noise.
"Gently!" Mrs Grant said.
"Your feet are not elephants."
She was very strict.
She never said "good" unless something was really good.
When Michael forgot to look in the mirror, she wrote it in her small black notebook.
When he drove too fast, she told him to stop the car and explained the rules again.
Some evenings, Michael came home tired and angry.
"She hates me," he told Helen.
"Nothing I do is right."
"Maybe she just wants you to be safe," Helen said.
Slowly, things started to get better.
After ten lessons, Michael could drive around the village without problems.
After twenty, he could drive on the main road.
He practised parking in the supermarket car park on Sunday mornings when it was empty.
He also studied the rules of the road every evening and passed the theory test on his first try.
He was proud of himself.
Finally, Mrs Grant said he was ready for the practical test.
It was booked for a Wednesday in October at nine o'clock in the morning, in the nearest town.
On the morning of the test, it was raining heavily.
Michael was very nervous.
The examiner was a young man with a clipboard who didn't smile at all.
They drove out of the test centre, and for the first ten minutes everything went well.
Michael checked his mirrors, used his signals and kept to the speed limit.
Then the examiner asked him to turn right at a busy crossroads.
Michael was thinking so hard about the turn that he didn't see the traffic lights change.
They had already turned red.
He drove straight through.
A car horn sounded loudly.
Michael's heart almost stopped.
Nobody was hurt, but when they returned to the test centre, the examiner gave him the bad news.
"I'm sorry," he said.
"You drove through a red light.
That is a serious mistake.
You have failed the test."
Michael felt terrible.
He had worked so hard, and it had all gone wrong in a few seconds.
He didn't want to talk to anyone that evening.
He thought about giving up.
"Maybe I'm just not a driver," he said to Helen.
"Maybe some people are too old to learn."
The next day, his phone rang.
It was Mrs Grant.
Michael expected her to be angry, but her voice was calm.
"I heard about the test," she said.
"Listen to me, Michael.
When I took my first test, I failed it too.
I hit the side of the road while I was parking.
The examiner said I would never be a good driver.
Now I have taught more than a thousand people."
Michael was surprised.
He had never imagined that Mrs Grant had failed anything.
"You are a careful driver," she continued.
"You only made one mistake because you were nervous.
If you give up now, you will always wonder.
Book another test.
We will practise crossroads until you can do them in your sleep."
So that is what they did.
For the next six weeks, Michael had two lessons every week.
Mrs Grant took him to every difficult crossroads in the area.
She also taught him a trick for his nerves: before every turn, he took one slow breath and said quietly to himself, "Mirror, signal, lights."
It seemed silly at first, but it worked.
His second test was in December.
The roads were cold and wet, and there was a little snow on the fields.
This time the examiner was an older woman with a friendly face.
Michael took a slow breath before every turn.
"Mirror, signal, lights," he whispered.
He stopped at every red light.
He even parked perfectly between two cars on a narrow street.
Back at the test centre, the examiner looked at her papers for a long moment.
Then she smiled.
"Congratulations, Mr Brooks," she said.
"You have passed."
Michael wanted to shout and jump, but he only said, "Thank you," and shook her hand.
When he came out, Mrs Grant was waiting by the door.
She didn't say anything at first.
Then, for the first time, she smiled.
"Good," she said.
"Really good."
That weekend, Michael drove Helen to the supermarket in their old red car.
On the way home, he took her for a drive along the coast.
"You know," Helen said, "I'm proud of you."
Michael smiled and kept his eyes on the road.
"Mirror, signal, lights," he said quietly, and he turned towards home.

title: A Week Without Phones
paragraphs: It was a grey Monday morning in March, and class 10B was waiting for their geography lesson.
Almost everyone was looking at a phone.
Some students were watching videos, some were sending messages and one boy was playing a game with the sound on.
Nobody noticed when their teacher, Mr Hughes, came into the room.
Mr Hughes stood at the front and waited.
After two minutes, he said loudly, "Good morning!"
A few students looked up.
Most didn't.
He wrote a number on the board: 7 hours 20 minutes.
"Last week, I asked you to check how much time you spend on your phones," he said.
"This is the average for this class.
Every day."
The room went quiet.
"That's not so much," said Jake, a tall boy who sat at the back.
But then Olivia, a quiet girl near the window, said, "It's almost as long as a school day."
Mr Hughes smiled.
"I'd like to suggest an experiment," he said.
"For one week, starting next Monday, nobody in this class uses a smartphone.
Not at school and not at home.
If you need to call your parents, you can use an old phone without the internet.
At the end of the week, we'll talk about what happened.
But everyone has to agree.
If one person says no, we won't do it."
There was a lot of noise.
Some students said it was impossible.
Jake said it was a crazy idea.
But Olivia raised her hand.
"I'll do it," she said.
Then her friend Mia agreed, and then another student, and another.
Finally, only Jake was left.
Everyone was looking at him.
"Fine," he said with a sigh.
"But I think it's a terrible idea."
That week, the students talked to their parents.
Most parents loved the idea.
Jake's mother was so happy that she offered to do it too.
On the first day of the experiment, everyone gave their smartphones to their parents in the morning.
Olivia felt strange on the bus to school.
Usually she listened to music and checked social media.
Now she just looked out of the window.
She noticed things that she had never seen before: a small bakery on the corner, a man walking five dogs at once, a beautiful old church.
She had taken this bus for three years.
At school, the breaks were very different.
Without phones, the students didn't know what to do with their hands.
For the first two days, many of them felt bored and nervous.
Jake kept touching his empty pocket.
"I feel like I've lost something," he said.
Some students worried that they were missing important news or messages from friends in other classes.
But by Wednesday, something had changed.
In the lunch break, a group of students started playing cards.
Someone had brought an old football, and a match started in the playground.
Mia and Olivia sat with two girls they had never really talked to before, and they discovered that they all loved the same books.
Jake had the biggest surprise.
On Wednesday afternoon, he was so bored at home that he opened his old guitar case.
His grandfather had given him the guitar for his twelfth birthday, but he had stopped playing because he never had time.
Now he had lots of time.
He played for two hours that evening, and again on Thursday.
There were problems too.
On Thursday, Mia got lost on her way to a friend's house because she couldn't use a map app.
She had to ask three people for directions.
One of them was an old lady who walked with her all the way to the right street.
"Young people never ask for help these days," the lady said.
"They only look at their phones."
Mia laughed and told her about the experiment.
Other things got better.
Most students said that they were sleeping much better.
They didn't look at screens late at night, so they fell asleep earlier.
Several students finished their homework faster.
One boy, Sam, read a whole novel in three days.
It was the first book he had finished since primary school.
On Friday afternoon, the week ended.
Mr Hughes put the chairs in a circle, and everyone talked about their experience.
Olivia said that she had felt more relaxed.
"I used to check my phone every five minutes," she said.
"I didn't even know why.
This week I felt calmer."
Mia told the story about the old lady.
"If I had had my phone, I would never have met her," she said.
Then Mr Hughes looked at Jake.
"And you, Jake?
Was it as terrible as you expected?"
Jake was quiet for a moment.
Then he picked up something from the floor.
It was his guitar.
"I've written a song," he said, a little embarrassed.
"It's about this week."
He played it for the class.
It wasn't perfect, but it was good, and everybody clapped loudly at the end.
On Saturday morning, the students got their smartphones back.
Most of them were happy to have them again.
They had a lot of messages, but nothing really important had happened.
Olivia noticed that she didn't feel excited when she turned her phone on.
She just felt normal.
The experiment had finished, but some things stayed.
The class decided to keep a new rule: no phones during lunch breaks.
Olivia stopped using her phone on the bus and kept looking out of the window.
Mia started asking people for directions sometimes, just for fun.
And Jake played his guitar every day.
A few weeks later, Jake performed his song at the school concert.
Before he started, he spoke into the microphone.
"This song was written during a week without phones," he said.
"So please, everyone, put your phones away and just listen."
And for three minutes, in a hall full of people, nobody looked at a screen.

title: The Lost Dog
paragraphs: The Parker family lived in a small house at the edge of a quiet town.
There were four of them: Mr and Mrs Parker, their daughter Lucy, who was twelve, and her little brother Ben, who was eight.
But if you asked Lucy, she always said there were five.
The fifth member of the family was Max, a big brown dog with soft ears and a very long tail.
The Parkers had found Max three years earlier.
He had been a tiny puppy then, and he had been sitting alone in a box outside a supermarket.
Lucy had cried until her parents agreed to take him home.
Since that day, Max had followed her everywhere.
He used to wait for her at the gate every afternoon when she came back from school.
One evening in October, the weather changed very quickly.
The sky became dark, and a strong wind started to blow.
By eight o'clock there was a terrible storm.
The rain was hitting the windows, and the trees in the garden were bending in the wind.
Then there was a loud crash of thunder, the loudest the children had ever heard.
Max hated thunder.
When the crash came, he jumped up and ran to the back door.
At that moment Mr Parker was coming in from the garden with some wood for the fire.
The door was open for only a few seconds, but it was enough.
Max ran past him into the dark and disappeared.
"Max!
Max, come back!" shouted Mr Parker.
He ran outside, but he couldn't see anything in the heavy rain.
He looked for twenty minutes and came back wet and worried.
"I'm sorry," he said quietly.
"I couldn't find him."
Lucy didn't sleep that night.
She lay in bed and listened to the storm.
"If he is cold and lost, he will be so frightened," she thought.
In the morning the storm had stopped, but Max had not come home.
The family started to search immediately.
Mrs Parker called the local vet and the police station.
Mr Parker drove slowly along every street in the town.
Lucy and Ben walked through the park and the fields behind the school, calling Max's name again and again.
Nobody had seen him.
In the afternoon, Lucy had an idea.
"Let's make posters," she said.
She found a nice photo of Max on her mother's phone, and they printed fifty copies.
Under the photo, in big letters, they wrote: "LOST DOG.
His name is Max.
He is brown, big and very friendly.
Please call us!"
They added their phone number.
Then the whole family went out and put the posters on trees, shop windows and bus stops.
Mrs Parker also posted the photo on social media.
She wrote a short message and asked people to share it.
By the evening, the post had been shared more than three hundred times.
Many people wrote kind comments.
"I hope you find him soon," wrote one woman.
"We will look in our garden," wrote another.
The phone started ringing the next day.
A man said that he had seen a brown dog near the train station.
The Parkers drove there at once, but it was a different dog, a small one with a red collar.
Later, a girl called and told them that a big dog was sleeping behind the sports centre.
Again, it wasn't Max.
Each time, Lucy's hope grew a little, and each time it broke again.
Three days passed, then four.
Ben stopped asking questions at dinner.
Lucy kept Max's old blue ball in her bag and held it when she felt sad.
Her teacher noticed that she was quiet at school.
"Don't give up," the teacher said.
"Dogs are clever.
They often find their way home."
On the fifth day, Mrs Parker received a message from a woman called Mrs Holmes.
She lived on a farm about ten kilometres outside the town.
"I think I have seen your dog," she wrote.
"There is a brown dog with my sheep.
He has been here for two days.
He won't come near me, but he is not hurting the animals.
He seems to be guarding them."
The family got into the car immediately.
Nobody spoke during the journey.
Lucy was holding the blue ball so tightly that her fingers hurt.
"What if it's not him again?" Ben whispered.
"Then we will keep looking," said his father.
The farm was on a green hill, and the sheep were walking slowly in a large field.
At first Lucy saw only white sheep.
Then, in the middle of them, she saw something brown.
It was lying in the grass with its head up, watching the sheep carefully.
Lucy opened the gate and shouted as loudly as she could.
"Max!"
The brown dog stood up.
For a second it didn't move.
Then its long tail started to wave, and it ran across the field so fast that the sheep jumped out of its way.
It was Max.
He jumped on Lucy and knocked her down into the wet grass, and he licked her face again and again.
Lucy was laughing and crying at the same time.
Ben threw his arms around Max's neck, and even Mr Parker had tears in his eyes.
Mrs Holmes came out of the house and smiled.
"So he really is yours," she said.
"He's a very good dog.
I have never seen a dog look after sheep like that.
If you ever want to sell him, I'll buy him!"
"Sorry," laughed Lucy.
"He's not for sale."
Nobody knew exactly how Max had got to the farm.
Mr Parker thought that the storm had frightened him so much that he had run for hours without stopping.
"Maybe he felt safe with the sheep," said Mrs Parker.
When they got home, Mrs Parker wrote a new post on social media.
"Max is home!
Thank you to everyone who helped us."
Then she put a new collar on Max with a small metal tag.
It had his name and their phone number on it.
That night there was a little rain, but no thunder.
Max slept on the floor next to Lucy's bed, with his old blue ball between his paws.
Lucy looked at him and smiled.
"Next time there's a storm," she said, "we'll stay inside together."

title: The Animal Shelter
paragraphs: Jack Wilson was fifteen, and he didn't like animals very much.
He didn't hate them, but he thought they were dirty, noisy and boring.
He preferred computer games, football and sleeping late on Saturdays.
So when his teacher, Mr Hughes, explained the new school project, Jack was not happy at all.
"This term, every student will do ten hours of volunteer work," said Mr Hughes.
"You can choose a library, a hospital, a sports club or a charity.
At the end, you will write a report and give a short presentation."
Most of Jack's friends quickly chose the sports club.
Jack waited too long, and when he looked at the list again, there was only one place left: the Green Hill Animal Shelter.
"Great," he said to himself.
"Ten hours with dogs and cats."
On his first Saturday, his mum drove him to the shelter.
It was an old building with a big garden behind it.
As soon as he opened the door, he heard dogs barking.
A woman in a green jacket came to meet him.
She had short dark hair and a friendly face.
"Hi, you must be Jack.
I'm Sarah, the manager," she said.
"Have you ever worked with animals before?"
"No," said Jack.
"And I'm not really an animal person."
Sarah only smiled.
"That's fine.
Most people say that on their first day."
She gave him a pair of gloves and a bucket.
His first job was to clean the dog kennels.
It was hard, smelly work, and after an hour his back hurt.
Then he had to wash the food bowls and carry heavy bags of dog food from the car to the storeroom.
When his mum picked him up, he said, "I've done two hours.
Only eight more to go."
The next Saturday, Sarah asked him to help with walking the dogs.
Most of them were excited and pulled on their leads.
But one dog stayed at the back of his kennel and didn't come out.
He was a thin grey dog with sad eyes and a scar on his nose.
"That's Bruno," said Sarah.
"He was found on the street two months ago.
Someone had left him tied to a tree in the middle of winter.
He doesn't trust people now.
Nobody has wanted to take him home."
Jack looked at Bruno for a long time.
He felt something strange inside, something he hadn't expected.
"Can I try?" he asked.
Sarah gave him a few dog biscuits.
"Don't go in.
Just sit near the door and talk to him quietly.
Let him come to you."
So Jack sat on the cold floor and talked.
He felt a bit silly at first.
He told Bruno about school, about his favourite football team and about his annoying little sister.
Bruno didn't move.
After twenty minutes, Jack put a biscuit on the floor and went away.
From then on, Jack spent part of every visit sitting outside Bruno's kennel.
On the third week, Bruno ate the biscuit while Jack was still there.
On the fourth week, he came close enough to smell Jack's hand.
On the fifth week, he let Jack touch his head.
Jack was so happy that he took a photo and sent it to his mum.
Something else was changing, too.
Jack started to notice how hard Sarah and the other volunteers worked.
They came in early, stayed late and never complained.
He learned how to give medicine to a cat, how to brush a dog and how to check if an animal was ill.
He even started reading about animals on the internet at home.
His parents were surprised.
"You used to say animals were boring," his dad said one evening.
Jack shrugged.
"I was wrong," he said.
By the time he had finished his ten hours, Jack didn't want to stop.
He kept going every Saturday.
One day he found Sarah in her office, looking at some papers with a worried face.
"Is everything OK?" he asked.
Sarah sighed.
"Not really.
The roof is leaking, and we need a new one before winter.
It will cost about three thousand pounds.
We don't have that money.
If we can't repair it, some kennels will have to close."
Jack thought about it all the way home.
That evening he called his friends Emma and Tom.
"I have an idea," he said.
"What if we organise a fundraising event at school?"
The next few weeks were very busy.
Jack and his friends talked to Mr Hughes, and the head teacher agreed to let them use the school hall.
They decided to have a cake sale, a raffle and a "Dog Show" where people could bring their own dogs.
Emma designed colourful posters.
Tom asked local shops to give prizes for the raffle.
Jack made a short video about the shelter, and Bruno was the star of it.
The video was shared on the school website and on social media.
Jack was nervous.
"What if nobody comes?" he asked Sarah.
"Then we'll eat a lot of cake," she said, laughing.
But on the day of the event, the hall was full.
Families came with children, grandparents and dogs of every size.
There was a tiny white dog in a pink jumper and a huge black dog who won the prize for "Best Smile".
People bought cakes, raffle tickets and T-shirts with the shelter's name on them.
At the end of the day, Jack and Sarah counted the money together.
Jack's hands were shaking.
"Three thousand four hundred and twenty pounds," Sarah said slowly.
Then she hugged him.
"Jack, you've saved the shelter."
But the best moment was still to come.
While they were packing up, a young couple came to Jack.
"We saw your video," the woman said.
"We would like to meet Bruno.
We have a big garden and a lot of time.
Do you think he would like us?"
Two weeks later, Bruno went to his new home.
Jack was happy for him, but he also felt a little sad.
On the last day, Bruno put his head on Jack's knee and looked at him with his grey eyes.
When Jack gave his presentation at school, he finished with these words: "I started this project because I had to.
I thought I didn't like animals.
Now I know that I just didn't know them." Then he smiled.
"And I'm still volunteering every Saturday."

title: The Night Train
paragraphs: Anna Clark was thirty-two and worked as a manager for a big company in London.
She was always busy.
She had meetings from morning to evening, she answered emails on the bus, and she never took a real holiday.
Her friends often told her that she worked too much, but Anna didn't listen.
In March, her company sent her to a conference in Vienna.
The conference was a success, and on Friday evening she had a flight back to London.
On Saturday morning she had an important meeting with a new client, so she couldn't be late.
But everything went wrong that afternoon.
Her last meeting finished late, and then her taxi got stuck in heavy traffic.
When she finally ran into the airport, the screen said "Gate closed".
She had missed her flight.
"There are no more flights to London tonight," the woman at the desk said.
"The next one is tomorrow at eleven."
Anna sat down on a bench and almost cried.
Then she looked at her phone.
There was a night train from Vienna that went across Europe.
If she took it, she could change trains in the morning and arrive in London by the afternoon.
It was not perfect, but it was better than nothing.
She bought a ticket and took a taxi to the station.
The train was old but comfortable.
Anna's ticket was for a small compartment with four seats which became beds at night.
When she opened the door, there was already one passenger inside.
He was an old man with white hair and a thick grey jumper.
He was drawing something in a notebook.
"Good evening," he said with a warm smile.
"I'm Henry.
It seems that we are travelling together tonight."
Anna said hello and sat down.
She opened her laptop immediately.
She wanted to prepare for her meeting.
But the Wi-Fi on the train didn't work, and after twenty minutes her battery was almost empty.
She closed the laptop and sighed.
"Bad day?" asked Henry.
"Terrible," said Anna.
She told him about the traffic and the missed flight.
"And now I'm going to be late for a very important meeting."
Henry nodded.
"I missed a train once, fifty years ago," he said.
"It was the best thing that ever happened to me."
Anna looked at him with surprise.
"Why?"
"I was twenty-two and I was going to Paris for a job interview," he explained.
"I had planned everything.
But I missed my train, so I had to wait in a small town in Switzerland for a whole day.
I went for a walk by a lake, and I met a young woman who was painting the mountains.
Her name was Maria.
I never went to the interview.
A year later, we got married."
Anna smiled for the first time that day.
"Is she travelling with you?"
Henry's face became a little sad.
"She died two years ago.
We had forty-seven happy years together.
Now I travel to the places we used to visit.
I draw them in this notebook.
It helps me remember her."
He showed her the notebook.
It was full of beautiful drawings: bridges, mountains, old churches and small cafés.
Under each drawing, he had written the name of the place and a short memory.
Anna turned the pages slowly.
They talked for hours.
The train was moving through the dark, and from time to time Anna saw the lights of small villages through the window.
Henry asked her about her life.
She told him about her job, her long hours and her small flat that she hardly ever saw in daylight.
"And what do you love doing?" he asked.
Anna opened her mouth, but she didn't know what to say.
"I used to love photography," she said at last.
"When I was at university, I took photos everywhere.
I even won a small competition once.
But I haven't taken a real photo for years.
I don't have time."
Henry looked at her kindly.
"If you don't make time for the things you love, nobody will make it for you," he said.
"Believe me.
Time goes faster than you think."
That night Anna lay in her narrow bed and couldn't sleep.
She kept thinking about Henry's words.
She remembered the old camera at the back of her wardrobe.
She remembered how happy she had been when she was walking around with it, looking for the perfect picture.
Early in the morning, she woke up and looked out of the window.
The train was passing through the mountains.
The sun was rising, and the snow on the tops of the mountains was pink and gold.
It was the most beautiful thing she had seen for a long time.
She took a photo with her phone, then another and another.
Henry was awake, too.
"Ah," he said.
"Now you have the right face.
That's the face of a photographer."
At the next station, Anna's phone found a signal at last.
There was an email from her client.
He said that he was ill and the meeting had been moved to Wednesday.
Anna laughed out loud.
All that stress, and the meeting wasn't even happening.
She thought for a moment.
Then she wrote an email to her boss.
She said that she would take a few days of holiday.
She hadn't had one for two years, and she knew her boss couldn't say no.
"Henry," she said, "where are you going next?"
"To a little town by a lake in Switzerland," he said, smiling.
"The place where I met Maria.
I go there every spring."
Anna didn't change trains for London.
Instead, she got off with Henry in Switzerland.
She bought a cheap camera in a shop near the station.
Then she spent three days walking by the lake and taking photos of boats, flowers, old houses and people's faces.
Henry showed her his favourite places, and in the evenings they ate soup in a small café and talked.
When she finally went back to London, she felt different.
She still worked hard, but she stopped answering emails after seven o'clock.
Every Sunday she went out with her camera.
In the summer, she sent Henry a letter with her best photo inside.
It showed an old man drawing in a notebook by a lake.
Under the photo she wrote: "Thank you for the missed flight."

title: Grandfather's Letters
paragraphs: Daniel was twenty-four when his grandfather, Walter, decided to move into a smaller flat.
The old family house had become too big for him, and the stairs were too difficult for his knees.
Daniel offered to help him with the move.
On the second day, Grandfather Walter asked him to clean the attic.
"I haven't been up there for ten years," he said.
"Throw away anything that is broken.
If you find something interesting, bring it down and show me."
The attic was dark and full of dust.
There were old chairs, boxes of books and a broken lamp.
Daniel worked for hours.
He was about to finish when he noticed a small wooden box in the corner, under an old coat.
It was locked, but the key was tied to the handle with a piece of string.
Inside the box, there were about fifty letters.
The paper was yellow and thin, and the envelopes had old stamps from Canada.
They were all addressed to the same person: Miss Rose Baker, 14 Mill Street, Bristol.
Daniel didn't know anyone called Rose Baker.
His grandmother's name had been Margaret.
He took the box downstairs.
His grandfather was sitting in the kitchen with a cup of tea.
When he saw the box, his face changed.
For a long moment he said nothing.
"Where did you find that?" he asked quietly.
"In the attic, under an old coat.
I'm sorry, Grandad.
Should I put it back?"
Walter shook his head slowly.
"No.
Sit down.
I think it's time you heard this story."
He picked up the first letter and touched it gently.
"When I was nineteen," he began, "I used to work at a bakery in Bristol.
I got up at four every morning and made bread.
Rose was the baker's daughter.
She used to sing while she worked, and she laughed at all my bad jokes.
We fell in love that summer."
Daniel listened in surprise.
He had never imagined his quiet, serious grandfather as a young man in love.
"But we were very poor," Walter went on.
"My father had lost his job, and my family needed money.
A friend told me that there was work in Canada, in the forests.
The pay was good.
So I decided to go for two years.
I promised Rose that I would come back and marry her.
I wrote to her every week."
"But these letters are here," said Daniel.
"Didn't she get them?"
"Read one," said his grandfather.
Daniel opened a letter carefully.
The handwriting was neat and a little old-fashioned.
"My dear Rose," it began.
"Today it snowed again.
The forest is so quiet that I can hear my own heart.
I work from morning until night, and I am always tired, but I think of you every evening.
I have already saved enough money for a small house.
Wait for me, my love."
On the back of the envelope there was a stamp: "Returned to sender.
Address unknown."
Daniel looked at the other envelopes.
Every one had the same stamp.
"I didn't understand," said Walter.
"Week after week, my letters came back.
I thought that Rose had forgotten me, or that she had found someone else.
I was heartbroken.
When I came home two years later, I went straight to Mill Street.
But the bakery had closed, and the family had moved away.
Nobody knew where they had gone."
"Did you ever find her?" Daniel asked.
"Not for a long time," said Walter.
"I looked for her for a year.
Then I met your grandmother, Margaret.
She was kind and clever, and she made me happy.
We had a good life together, and I loved her very much.
But I never threw away these letters."
Daniel was silent.
He could see that his grandfather's eyes were wet.
Then Walter smiled a little.
"But the story isn't finished," he said.
"About five years ago, after your grandmother died, I got a phone call from a woman.
She said that her name was Helen and that she was Rose's daughter.
Rose had died, and Helen had found my name in her mother's diary."
"What did the diary say?" asked Daniel.
"It explained everything.
Rose's father had had serious money problems.
The bakery was sold, and the family had to leave Bristol very quickly.
They moved to Scotland.
Rose had written to me many times, but she had sent her letters to the wrong address in Canada.
The company had moved me to another camp, and nobody had sent my post on.
We had both been writing, and we had both been waiting.
We just never found each other."
Daniel didn't know what to say.
"That's so sad," he said at last.
"Yes," said Walter.
"But Helen told me something else.
Rose had a happy life too.
She married a good man and had three children.
And on her last birthday, she told Helen about a boy from the bakery who used to make her laugh.
She said that she had never forgotten him."
They sat together in the quiet kitchen for a long time.
Outside, it was getting dark.
That evening, Daniel read all the letters, one by one.
In them, he met a young man he had never known.
This young man was brave, funny and full of dreams.
He wrote about bears in the forest, the cold Canadian winter and the friends he had made at the camp.
He described the house he wanted to build, with a garden full of roses.
Before Daniel went home, he asked his grandfather a question.
"Grandad, can I keep the letters?
I don't want them to be lost again."
Walter thought for a moment, then nodded.
"Yes.
Take them.
But promise me one thing.
If you ever love someone, tell them clearly, and don't wait too long.
Life doesn't always give you a second chance."
A few months later, Daniel visited his grandfather in his new flat.
He brought a present.
He had scanned all the letters and made them into a beautiful book with a dark blue cover.
On the first page, he had written: "The Letters of Walter Evans, 1958 to 1960.
A love story."
His grandfather held the book for a long time.
Then he looked up and smiled.
"You know," he said, "if I hadn't gone to Canada, you wouldn't be here.
Life is strange like that."
Daniel smiled back.
Later, the blue book stood on the shelf next to a photo of his grandmother, Margaret.
