title: A Year in Japan
paragraphs: When Kate Morgan finished university, she didn't know what to do next.
She had studied history, but she didn't want to work in an office.
One evening she saw an advert online: "Teach English in Japan for one year.
No experience needed."
She had always been interested in Japan.
She had read books about it and watched Japanese films, but she had never been to Asia.
She applied the same night.
Two months later, she was sitting on a plane to Osaka.
She felt excited and nervous at the same time.
"What if I don't like it?" she thought.
"What if nobody understands me?"
Her new job was at a secondary school in a small town near Osaka.
The school had given her a tiny flat near the station.
It had one room, a small kitchen and a bathroom with a very complicated toilet.
The toilet had more buttons than her phone, and all the instructions were in Japanese.
On her first night, she pressed the wrong button and got water all over her clothes.
She laughed so much that she forgot how tired she was.
The first few weeks were difficult.
Everything was new.
In the supermarket, she couldn't read the labels, so she often bought the wrong things.
Once she bought a packet of what she thought was sugar, but it was salt.
She put it in her coffee and almost spat it out.
At the train station, she got lost again and again because the station was so big.
At school, she worked with a Japanese teacher of English called Mr Tanaka.
He was polite and serious, and at first Kate found him a little cold.
On her first day, she gave him a big friendly hug.
He stood very still and his face turned red.
Later, a younger teacher called Yuki explained that people in Japan usually bow when they meet.
They don't hug colleagues.
"Don't worry," said Yuki, smiling.
"He will remember it forever, but he isn't angry."
Kate learned many rules like this.
She learned that you take off your shoes before you go into someone's house.
She learned that you shouldn't eat while you are walking in the street.
She learned that people are very quiet on trains and that nobody talks on the phone there.
She had never thought about these things before.
At home in England, people did things differently.
Sometimes she felt very lonely.
In the evenings she sat in her small flat and called her family on video.
"I miss you all," she told her mum one night.
"I miss real bread and I miss being able to read things."
Her mum listened and said, "If it's still this hard after three months, you can come home.
But give it a chance."
The turning point came in her third month.
One of the students in her class was a quiet boy called Kenji.
He never spoke in lessons.
He always looked at his desk when Kate asked him a question.
The other teachers said that he was shy and that he didn't like English.
One day, Kate noticed that Kenji had drawn a picture in the corner of his notebook.
It was a perfect drawing of a famous footballer from England.
"Do you like football?" she asked.
For the first time, Kenji looked up.
"Yes," he said quietly.
"Liverpool." Kate smiled.
Her father had supported Liverpool all his life.
The next week, Kate brought some English football magazines to class.
She made a lesson about sports, and the students had to describe their favourite players.
Kenji spoke for two minutes without stopping.
His English wasn't perfect, but everyone listened.
When he finished, the class clapped.
Mr Tanaka looked at Kate and gave her a small nod.
Later he told her that it had been an excellent lesson.
After that, things became easier.
Kate started taking Japanese lessons twice a week.
She learned to read simple words and to order food in restaurants.
Yuki became her best friend.
They went to hot springs together, visited old temples in Kyoto and ate street food at summer festivals.
Yuki's grandmother taught Kate how to make rice balls and how to wear a kimono.
Even Mr Tanaka changed.
Or maybe Kate understood him better.
One evening, the teachers went out for dinner together.
After two glasses of beer, Mr Tanaka started singing old English pop songs in a karaoke bar.
He had a terrible voice, but he knew every word.
Kate laughed until she cried.
"When I was a student," he told her, "I used to dream about visiting London.
I never had the chance."
Kate promised to show him around if he ever came.
In winter, Kate made her biggest mistake.
She was invited to Yuki's family's house for New Year.
She wanted to bring a present, so she bought a beautiful set of four white plates.
When Yuki's mother opened the box, there was a short, strange silence.
Later Yuki explained that the number four sounds like the word for "death" in Japanese.
Kate felt terrible, but Yuki's mother just smiled and said, "Now we know you will never forget this rule."
The year went very fast.
Suddenly it was spring again, and the cherry trees were covered in pink flowers.
Kate's contract was almost finished.
The school had asked her to stay for another year, but her family wanted her to come home.
She didn't know what to do.
On her last day at school, the students gave her a large card.
Every student had written a message in English.
Kenji's message was the longest.
He wrote that he had decided to study English at university.
"Because of you, I am not afraid to speak now," he had written.
Kate read it on the train home and cried quietly, like a true Japanese passenger, without making any noise.
In the end, Kate went back to England for the summer.
But in September, she returned to Japan for a second year.
When people ask her what she learned, she always gives the same answer.
"I learned that mistakes are not a problem.
If you are kind and you keep trying, people will help you.
And I learned that home is not only one place."

title: The Startup Idea
paragraphs: Every Saturday morning, Jake and his best friend Nina used to go to the farmers' market in their small town.
They would buy fresh bread, cheese and vegetables, and then they would sit in a café and talk about their dreams.
Jake was a software developer who worked for a large bank.
Nina had studied business and worked in the marketing department of a supermarket chain.
Both of them were bored with their jobs.
One Saturday in March, they arrived at the market a little late.
The man who sold the best honey had already gone home, and the bakery stall had sold all its bread.
"If only we had known," Nina said.
"We could have come earlier."
An old farmer who was packing his boxes heard her.
"That happens every week," he told them.
"People don't know what we have or when we finish.
And when it rains, half of them stay at home, and we throw away food."
On the way to the café, Jake was unusually quiet.
Then he stopped in the middle of the street.
"What if there was an app for this?" he asked.
"Farmers could show what they are selling that day.
People could order in advance and pick their bags up at the stall.
Nothing would be wasted."
Nina looked at him for a long moment.
"That's actually a brilliant idea," she said.
For the next three months, they spent every evening and weekend on the project.
Jake wrote the code, while Nina talked to the farmers and planned how to advertise the app.
They called it "Market Basket".
Not everybody was enthusiastic.
Some of the older farmers had never used a smartphone, and one of them said he would rather close his stall than learn.
But Nina was patient.
She visited them again and again, explained everything slowly and helped them to take photos of their products.
By the summer, twelve farmers had agreed to try the app.
The first version was tested by about two hundred people from the town.
The results were better than they had expected.
Orders were coming in every Friday night, and the farmers were selling more than before.
The old farmer who had complained about the rain told Nina that he had not thrown away a single box of tomatoes for a month.
There was only one problem: money.
Jake and Nina had been paying for everything themselves.
The servers, the design and the advertising had cost much more than they had planned.
By September, Nina had spent nearly all her savings.
Jake had borrowed money from his parents, and he felt terrible about it.
"We can't go on like this," he said one evening.
"Either we find an investor, or we stop."
A friend of Nina's told them about a competition for new businesses in the city.
Five teams would be chosen to present their ideas to a group of investors, and the winner would receive fifty thousand pounds.
They sent an application, and two weeks later they were invited to take part.
Nina was delighted.
Jake was terrified.
He had never spoken in front of a large audience before.
They prepared for the pitch for three weeks.
Nina wrote the presentation, and Jake practised his part in front of the mirror.
On the day of the competition, they arrived early.
The other teams looked very professional, and they were wearing expensive suits.
Jake suddenly felt like a schoolboy.
The pitch was a disaster.
First, the projector didn't work with Jake's laptop, and they lost five minutes trying to fix it.
Then Jake forgot half of what he had prepared.
When one of the investors, a woman called Mrs Grant, asked him how they would make money, he couldn't give a clear answer.
"Well, we haven't completely decided yet," he said.
Another investor asked whether the app would work in big cities.
Nina tried to answer, but she could see that they were not convinced.
After ten minutes, they were thanked politely and asked to leave.
They didn't win.
They weren't even mentioned at the end.
On the train home, neither of them spoke for a long time.
Finally, Jake said, "I wish I hadn't agreed to do this.
If I had been better prepared, we might have had a chance."
Nina shook her head.
"It wasn't only you.
We had been working so hard on the app that we forgot to think about the business.
They were right to ask those questions."
For a week, they didn't talk about Market Basket at all.
Jake went to work, came home and watched television.
He was seriously thinking about giving up.
Then, on Saturday morning, Nina phoned him.
"Come to the market," she said.
"I want to show you something."
When Jake arrived, the market was busier than he had ever seen it.
Nina pointed at the stalls.
Almost every farmer had a small sign with the Market Basket logo on it.
A young mother was collecting her bag of vegetables, and she was showing her friend how to use the app.
"Look at this," Nina said.
"People are using it every week, and we haven't spent a penny on advertising for a month.
The idea works.
We just need to explain it better."
That afternoon, they sat in their usual café with a notebook.
They made a list of all the questions the investors had asked, and they tried to answer every one honestly.
They decided that the farmers would pay a small amount for each order, and that shoppers would use the app for free.
They also found out that there were more than five hundred farmers' markets in the country.
Suddenly, their small idea did not look so small.
Three weeks later, something unexpected happened.
Nina received an email from Mrs Grant, the investor who had asked the difficult question at the competition.
She wrote that she had been thinking about their app since that day.
Her parents had a farm, and she had told them about Market Basket.
They had downloaded it, and they liked it very much.
She asked whether Jake and Nina would be interested in meeting her for coffee.
This time, they were ready.
They brought their notebook, the numbers from the last six months and a short video in which three farmers talked about how the app had changed their week.
Jake explained the business plan clearly and calmly.
When Mrs Grant asked how they would make money, he smiled.
"I'm glad you asked that again," he said.
"We've thought about it a lot since the last time."
Mrs Grant laughed.
At the end of the meeting, she told them that she would like to invest in their company.
It was not fifty thousand pounds, but it was enough to pay for the servers for a year and to bring the app to three more towns.
A year later, Market Basket was used at forty markets, and Jake and Nina had left their old jobs.
They had made many mistakes, and they knew they would make more.
But every Saturday they still went to the market in their small town, bought fresh bread and sat in the same café.
"Do you know what?" Jake said one morning.
"If we had won that competition, we would never have learned so much."
Nina raised her coffee cup.
"To failing," she said.
"The first time."

title: The Old Bookshop
paragraphs: Emma was twenty-nine and lived in a small flat in London, where she worked as an accountant for a big insurance company.
She had a good salary, but she spent most of her days looking at numbers on a screen.
One rainy Tuesday in October, she received a phone call from a lawyer.
Her great-aunt Margaret had died, and she had left Emma something in her will: an old bookshop in a seaside town called Hollow Bay.
Emma had not visited Aunt Margaret for nearly fifteen years.
When she was a child, she used to spend every summer with her.
She would sit for hours in the corner of the shop, reading adventure stories, while her aunt served customers and told her the names of all the authors.
Then Emma had grown up, gone to university and become busy.
She had always intended to visit again, but she had never found the time.
Now it was too late, and she felt guilty.
The following weekend, she took the train to Hollow Bay.
The shop was in a narrow street near the harbour.
It was smaller than she had remembered.
The paint on the door was coming off, and the sign above the window was so faded that it was hard to read the name: "Margaret's Books".
Inside, it smelled of old paper and dust.
There were books everywhere, on the shelves, on the floor and in boxes on the stairs.
An elderly man was sitting behind the counter, reading a newspaper.
He stood up when she came in.
"You must be Emma," he said.
"I'm Arthur.
I've been helping your aunt here for twenty years.
She told me you would come."
He made her a cup of tea in the tiny kitchen at the back and showed her the accounts.
Emma looked at them with the eyes of an accountant, and her heart sank.
The shop had been losing money for years.
Most months, fewer than a hundred books were sold.
"Why did she keep it open?" Emma asked.
Arthur smiled sadly.
"Because she loved it.
And because the town needed it.
Children used to come here after school.
Old people came here to talk.
It was more than a shop for her."
He paused.
"But I won't lie to you.
Unless something changes, it will close within a year."
On Monday, a man from a property company called Emma.
He had heard that she had inherited the building, and he offered her a large amount of money for it.
His company wanted to turn the shop into a holiday flat.
Emma did the calculations on the train back to London.
With that money, she could pay off most of her loan for her flat.
It was the sensible thing to do.
She told the man that she would give him an answer in two weeks.
But she couldn't stop thinking about the shop.
At night she dreamed of the corner where she used to read.
At work she found herself searching online for information about small bookshops that had survived.
She read about shops that had been saved by organising events, opening cafés or selling books online.
One evening she called her friend Leila, who ran a small bakery.
"Am I crazy?" Emma asked.
"I'm an accountant.
I don't know how to run a shop."
"You know more than you think," Leila said.
"You understand money, and you love books.
If I were you, I would at least try.
You can always sell it later.
But if you sell it now, you can never get it back."
Emma thought about those words for a long time.
The next Friday, she asked her manager whether she could work from home for three months.
To her surprise, he agreed, as long as she came to the office once a month.
Emma packed two suitcases and moved into the small flat above the bookshop.
Arthur was so happy that he almost cried.
The first weeks were very hard.
Emma got up early to do her accounting work and spent the afternoons and evenings in the shop.
She and Arthur sorted thousands of books.
They threw away the ones that had been damaged by water and put the rest in order.
Emma painted the door bright blue and had the sign repaired.
She set up a website and started selling rare books online, which brought in some money immediately.
Arthur, who had never used a computer, was amazed.
"Your aunt would have loved this," he said.
Then Emma had another idea.
She remembered how much she had enjoyed listening to her aunt as a child.
She put an advertisement in the local newspaper for a story hour every Saturday morning.
On the first Saturday, only three children came.
Emma was disappointed, but she read to them anyway.
The next week, there were nine.
By December, the shop was so full on Saturday mornings that some parents had to wait outside.
Other people started to come too.
A retired teacher asked whether she could run a book club in the evenings.
A group of teenagers asked if they could use the back room to write and draw.
Emma bought a coffee machine and some second-hand armchairs.
Slowly, the shop came back to life.
People who had not been inside for years told her stories about Aunt Margaret, and Emma learned things about her aunt that she had never known.
However, by the end of the three months, the numbers were still not good enough.
The shop was losing less money than before, but it was still losing money.
The man from the property company called again.
He said that his offer would only be valid for one more week.
Emma sat in the empty shop that evening and cried.
She wished she had more time.
She wished she had come back while her aunt was still alive.
On Saturday morning, after the story hour, a woman with a little boy waited until everyone had gone.
She introduced herself as Mrs Collins, the head of the local school.
She told Emma that the school library had been closed because there was no money for it.
"My son has started reading because of you," she said.
"Would you be interested in working with the school?
We have a small budget from the town council for reading programmes.
It isn't much, but we could pay you to run classes here twice a week."
That was not all.
The teenagers had secretly started an online campaign called "Save Margaret's Books".
In just a few days, more than a thousand people had signed it, and some of them had sent small donations.
A journalist from a national newspaper wrote an article about the shop, and online orders tripled in a week.
Emma called the property company and told them that the shop was not for sale.
Then she went back to London, spoke to her manager and asked to work part-time.
He wasn't happy, but he accepted her decision.
A year later, Margaret's Books was not rich, but it was paying for itself.
Emma still did some accounting work three days a week, and Arthur still made tea in the tiny kitchen.
Every Saturday morning, Emma sat in the corner where she had read as a child and opened a book for a room full of children.
Above the counter, she had hung a photo of her aunt.
Sometimes, when the shop was quiet, Emma looked at it and said, "Thank you."
She was sure that, wherever she was, Aunt Margaret was smiling.

title: The First Marathon
paragraphs: At school, Oliver had hated sport more than anything.
He was always the last person to be chosen for a team, and he would hide in the changing room during football matches.
When he grew up, he got a job in an office as a data analyst and stopped doing any exercise at all.
By the age of thirty-four, he spent nine hours a day sitting at a desk and most evenings sitting on the sofa.
He took the lift even when he only needed to go up one floor.
Everything changed one Monday in January.
His company had organised free health checks for all employees.
The nurse who examined Oliver looked at the results for a long time.
"Your blood pressure is too high," she said.
"And you are about fifteen kilos heavier than you should be.
If you don't change your lifestyle, you might have serious problems in ten years."
Oliver walked back to his desk feeling shocked.
His father had had a heart attack at fifty, and he did not want the same thing to happen to him.
That evening, he told his colleague and friend Grace about it.
Grace was a keen runner who had already finished three marathons.
"Why don't you start running with me?" she suggested.
"We could go twice a week after work." Oliver laughed.
"Me?
I can't even run for a bus."
But Grace didn't give up.
She kept asking him every day until he finally agreed, mainly to make her stop.
The first run was terrible.
Grace had planned a gentle route of three kilometres in the park.
After five minutes, Oliver had to stop.
His face was red, his legs were burning, and he felt as if his lungs were on fire.
"This is a mistake," he said, breathing heavily.
"I'm just not made for running."
Grace explained that everyone found it hard at the beginning.
She showed him how to run slowly and walk for a minute whenever he needed to.
"The secret isn't running fast," she said.
"It's not stopping completely."
Oliver went back the following week, and then the week after.
Slowly, something surprising happened.
He started to look forward to the runs.
After a month, he could run three kilometres without walking.
After three months, he could run eight.
He had lost six kilos, and he was sleeping better than he had for years.
He had even started taking the stairs at work, which his colleagues found very funny.
In May, Grace told him that she had registered for the city marathon in October.
"You should do it too," she said.
Oliver thought she was joking.
A marathon was forty-two kilometres.
Until that spring, he had never run more than one.
But that night he couldn't sleep.
He kept thinking about what the nurse had said and about the boy who used to hide in the changing room.
At two in the morning, he got up, opened his laptop and registered before he could change his mind.
Grace helped him to make a training plan.
He would run four times a week, and every Sunday he would do a long run, which would get a little longer each week.
He bought proper running shoes and started to eat more healthily.
He gave up the chocolate bars he used to eat every afternoon at his desk.
His mother, who had been worried about his health for years, was so pleased that she told all her friends about it.
By August, Oliver had been training for seven months, and he had just completed his first thirty-kilometre run.
He felt stronger than ever.
Then, one wet Sunday morning, it all went wrong.
He was running down a hill in the park when he slipped on some wet leaves.
He felt a sharp pain in his right knee and fell to the ground.
He couldn't stand up, and a man who was walking his dog had to call a taxi for him.
The doctor told him that he had damaged a ligament in his knee.
"It isn't very serious," she said, "but you must rest for at least four weeks.
No running at all."
Oliver asked whether he would be able to run the marathon.
The doctor looked at him doubtfully.
"I would not recommend it," she said.
"If you had been injured earlier in the year, you would have had time to recover.
Now, I'm afraid it will be very difficult."
The next few weeks were the hardest of all.
Oliver sat at home with his leg on a cushion and felt sorry for himself.
He stopped answering Grace's messages.
He started eating chocolate again.
"I wish I had never started," he told his mother on the phone.
"I should have known that I'm not a runner.
People like me don't run marathons."
His mother was quiet for a moment.
Then she said, "Do you remember what you were like in January?
You couldn't walk up the stairs without stopping.
Look at what you have already done."
Her words stayed with him.
The next day, he called Grace and apologised for ignoring her.
She came round with a bag of fruit and a plan.
She had spoken to a physiotherapist who was a friend of hers.
He had told her that Oliver could not run, but he could swim and ride an exercise bike, and this would help him to keep fit without hurting his knee.
Oliver started going to the swimming pool every morning before work.
It was boring, but it was better than doing nothing.
After five weeks, the physiotherapist examined his knee and said that he could start running again, very slowly.
There were only four weeks left before the marathon.
Oliver knew that he was not as fit as he had been in August.
He asked the physiotherapist directly whether he should run or not.
The physiotherapist said that it was his decision, but that if he ran, he must go slowly and stop immediately if his knee hurt.
"Your goal isn't a good time," he said.
"Your goal is to finish."
On the morning of the marathon, it was cold and grey.
Thousands of runners were waiting at the start line, and music was playing loudly.
Oliver felt sick with nerves.
Grace gave him a hug.
"Remember," she said, "it's not about running fast.
It's about not stopping completely."
Then the race began.
The first twenty kilometres went better than he had expected.
He ran slowly and steadily, and his knee felt fine.
Crowds of people stood along the streets, shouting and clapping for runners they didn't even know.
At kilometre thirty, however, his legs became heavy, and his knee started to ache.
At kilometre thirty-five, he stopped and walked.
He was sure that he would have to give up.
Then he heard someone call his name.
His mother was standing at the side of the road, holding a sign that said "GO OLIVER!
YOU ARE A RUNNER!"
Beside her were half the people from his office, including his manager, who had never said a kind word to him in four years.
Oliver felt tears in his eyes.
He started running again, slowly, one step at a time.
He crossed the finish line five hours and forty minutes after he had started.
Many people had finished much earlier, but he did not care at all.
A volunteer put a medal around his neck, and Grace, who had finished an hour before him, ran over and hugged him.
"You did it," she said.
Oliver couldn't speak.
He just held the medal and smiled.
Now, the medal hangs on the wall above Oliver's desk at work.
Sometimes new colleagues ask him about it, and he tells them the story.
He always ends it the same way.
"Don't wait until you are ready," he says.
"Just start, and don't stop completely."

title: Lost Luggage
paragraphs: Daniel Ross had worked as a sales manager for a small company that made medical equipment for nearly ten years.
He was good at his job, but he had never had a chance like this one.
A large hospital group in Lisbon was looking for a new supplier, and Daniel's company had been invited to present its products.
If the hospital chose them, it would be the biggest contract in the company's history.
His boss had told him that he trusted him completely.
That made Daniel even more nervous.
He had prepared for weeks.
He had practised the presentation so many times that he could do it in his sleep.
In his suitcase, he had packed his best suit, a new white shirt and, most importantly, a small sample of the company's newest product, a portable heart monitor.
He had decided to put the sample in his suitcase because he was worried that it would be stopped at security if he took it in his hand luggage.
His flight left on Wednesday afternoon, and the presentation was at nine o'clock on Thursday morning.
The flight was delayed for an hour, but Daniel didn't mind.
He used the time to read his notes again.
When he landed in Lisbon, it was already dark.
He waited at the baggage carousel with the other passengers.
One by one, they collected their bags and left.
After forty minutes, the carousel stopped.
Daniel was standing there alone.
His suitcase had not arrived.
He went to the lost luggage office, where a tired young woman was sitting behind a desk.
She typed his name into her computer and frowned.
"I'm sorry, sir," she said.
"It seems that your suitcase was put on the wrong plane in London.
At the moment, we think it is in Lyon."
Daniel stared at her.
"In France?
When will it be here?"
She explained that it would probably be sent to Lisbon the next afternoon.
"But my presentation is tomorrow morning," Daniel said.
"Everything I need is in that suitcase."
The woman gave him a form to fill in and a small bag with a toothbrush and a T-shirt.
"I really am sorry," she said.
"I wish I could do more."
It was nearly midnight when Daniel arrived at his hotel.
He was wearing jeans, an old jumper and trainers, which he had put on for the flight because they were comfortable.
He sat on the bed and looked at himself in the mirror.
He couldn't present to the directors of a hospital group dressed like this.
And without the heart monitor, he could only show them pictures.
If only he had put the sample in his hand luggage, he thought.
He would have had to explain it at security, but at least he would have it now.
He called his boss, Mrs Hall, in London.
He expected her to be angry, but she was calm.
"Don't panic," she said.
"You know the product better than anyone.
The suit is not important.
Do what you can, and call me after the meeting."
Her words helped a little, but Daniel still couldn't sleep.
At seven in the morning, he went down to the reception desk.
A young man called Tiago was working there.
Daniel explained what had happened and asked whether there was a clothes shop nearby.
Tiago looked at his watch.
"Most shops open at ten," he said.
"That's too late for you."
He thought for a moment.
Then he picked up the phone and spoke quickly in Portuguese.
When he put the phone down, he was smiling.
"My uncle has a small tailor's shop two streets from here," he said.
"He usually opens at nine, but he will open early for you.
He says he has some suits that people ordered but never collected."
Twenty minutes later, Daniel was standing in a tiny shop full of fabric, while an old man with glasses was measuring his arms.
Tiago's uncle didn't speak much English, but he didn't need to.
He brought out a dark grey suit, looked at Daniel, shook his head and brought another one.
The second suit fitted almost perfectly.
He took in the trousers a little, ironed a white shirt and even lent Daniel a tie.
When Daniel tried to pay, the price he was asked for was much lower than he had expected.
"For good luck," the old man said in careful English.
Daniel still had one problem: the heart monitor.
In the taxi to the hospital, he called a colleague in London and asked her to send him the newest video of the product.
He had been planning to use the real sample, so he hadn't put the video in his presentation.
His colleague promised to email it to him immediately.
The video arrived as the taxi stopped outside the hospital.
At the reception, a woman told him that the meeting room was on the fifth floor.
As he was waiting for the lift, a tall man in a white coat started a conversation with him.
He asked Daniel where he was from and why he had come.
Daniel was so nervous that he told him everything: the lost suitcase, the tailor, the borrowed tie.
The man laughed.
"That is quite a story," he said.
"Good luck with your presentation."
Then he got out on the third floor.
The meeting room was large and bright, and six people were sitting around the table.
The director, a serious woman called Dr Ferreira, invited Daniel to begin.
He started by apologising that he could not show them the real product.
He explained that it had been sent to France by mistake.
A few of the directors smiled.
Then he showed them the video and talked about the heart monitor in detail.
He explained how it worked, how much it cost and how it could be used by patients at home.
He answered all their questions clearly.
For the first time since he had landed, he felt confident.
Near the end of the meeting, the door opened, and the tall man from the lift came in.
He sat down and listened.
Daniel realised with a shock that he was one of the hospital's senior heart doctors.
When Daniel had finished, the doctor spoke.
"This morning, Mr Ross told me that he had lost his suitcase and that he had found a suit in a few hours with the help of strangers," he said.
"I think that a person who can solve problems like that will also solve our problems if something goes wrong with his equipment.
That matters to me more than a product sample."
Dr Ferreira said they would make their decision within a week.
Daniel thanked them and left the building.
He felt that the meeting had gone well, but he didn't want to hope too much.
That afternoon, his suitcase was finally delivered to the hotel.
He opened it and found the heart monitor, safe and undamaged.
He took it back to the hospital the next morning so that the doctors could test it before he flew home.
On the way to the airport, he stopped at the tailor's shop to return the tie.
Tiago's uncle refused to take it.
"Keep it," he said.
"Next time, you will tell me if it was lucky."
Eight days later, Mrs Hall called him into her office.
The hospital group had signed the contract.
Daniel's company would supply heart monitors to twelve of its hospitals for the next five years.
"Well done," she said.
"Next time, though, maybe pack a spare shirt in your hand luggage."
Daniel laughed.
He still wears the grey tie whenever he has an important meeting.
And every Christmas, he sends a card to a small tailor's shop in Lisbon, thanking the strangers who had helped him when everything had gone wrong.

title: The Wrong Email
paragraphs: Laura had been working at a software company in Manchester for two years.
She worked in the customer support team, which answered questions from people who were having problems with the company's programs.
Laura was good at her job.
She was patient, polite and always ready to help.
But inside, she was becoming more and more unhappy.
Her team had too much work, and nobody seemed to notice.
The problem had started six months earlier, when the company had changed its computer system.
The new system was slow, and it often crashed.
Customers were angry because they had to wait for days for an answer.
Laura and her colleagues had been working late almost every evening.
Two of them had already left the company, and they had not been replaced.
Laura had tried to explain the situation to her manager, Mr Price, several times.
Each time, he had listened politely and then said, "We all have to work harder at the moment."
One Thursday evening in November, Laura was still at her desk at half past seven.
She had been answering emails since eight in the morning, and she had not had a proper lunch.
Her best friend at work, Sophie, had gone home an hour earlier.
Laura decided to write her a message to explain how she felt.
She wrote quickly, without thinking too much.
"I can't do this any more," she wrote.
"Mr Price has no idea what is happening in our team.
He sits in his office all day and goes to meetings about 'customer happiness', but he has never spent a single hour answering customers himself.
The new system is a disaster, and everybody knows it except the people who bought it.
If things don't change soon, I'm going to start looking for another job.
Honestly, I sometimes wonder whether anyone upstairs even knows our names."
She pressed "Send", closed her laptop and went home.
She felt a little better.
The next morning, Laura was drinking her coffee when her phone started to buzz.
It buzzed again, and then again.
She had eleven new messages.
The first one was from Sophie.
It said only, "Laura, CHECK YOUR SENT EMAILS.
NOW."
Laura opened her laptop with shaking hands.
Her heart almost stopped.
She had not sent the message to Sophie.
When she had started typing the name, the computer had suggested "Staff - All", the list that was used for company announcements.
She had clicked on it without looking.
Her email had been sent to all three hundred and forty people in the company, including Mr Price, the directors and the head of the whole company, Mrs Okafor.
For a few minutes, Laura just sat there.
She wanted to disappear.
She thought about calling in sick.
She even thought about never going back to the office at all.
"If only I had checked the address," she said to herself again and again.
"If I had waited until the morning, none of this would have happened."
But Laura was not the kind of person who ran away from problems.
She took a deep breath and called her mother, who had worked as a nurse for thirty years and always gave practical advice.
Her mother listened carefully.
"You can't change what you wrote," she said.
"But you can decide what you do next.
Did you write anything that wasn't true?" Laura thought about it.
"No," she said.
"Some of it was rude, but it was all true."
"Then go in, apologise for the way you said it, and don't apologise for what you meant," her mother said.
When Laura walked into the office, the room went quiet.
Some people looked at her with sympathy.
Others were obviously trying not to laugh.
A man from the finance department, whom she had never spoken to before, gave her a thumbs up as she passed.
On her desk there was a note from Mr Price.
It said that he wanted to see her in his office at ten o'clock.
Laura spent the next hour preparing what she would say.
At ten o'clock, she knocked on his door.
Mr Price was sitting behind his desk, and he did not look happy.
To her surprise, Mrs Okafor was also in the room.
Laura spoke first.
She said that she was very sorry.
She explained that the email had been meant for a friend, and that she should never have written about Mr Price in that way.
"It was unprofessional, and it was unkind," she said.
"I'm truly sorry for that."
Then she paused.
"But I can't say that I'm sorry about the rest of it.
Our team is exhausted.
We have been asking for help for months.
I should have said it differently, but I believe it needed to be said."
Mr Price's face went red.
He started to say something, but Mrs Okafor raised her hand.
She asked Laura how many hours her team had been working each week.
Then she asked how long customers usually had to wait for an answer, and how many people had left the team.
Laura answered every question honestly.
She had the numbers on her phone, because she had been recording them for weeks.
Mrs Okafor wrote everything down.
At the end of the meeting, Mrs Okafor thanked her and told her that she could go back to work.
Laura had no idea what was going to happen.
For the rest of the day, she was sure that she would be fired.
On Monday morning, everybody in the company received another email.
This time it was from Mrs Okafor.
She wrote that she had been told about serious problems in the customer support team.
She admitted that the directors had not realised how bad the situation had become.
She wrote that two new people would be hired for the team immediately, and that the computer system would be checked by an independent expert.
She also announced that every manager, including herself, would spend one day a month working in customer support.
At the end of the email, she wrote: "Sometimes we learn the most important things in the most unexpected ways."
Laura was not fired.
Mr Price was moved to a different department a few weeks later.
Before he left, he came to her desk.
Laura expected him to be angry, but he was calm.
He told her that he had been upset by her email, but that he had thought about it a lot.
"I should have listened to you," he said.
"If I had spent more time with your team, I would have seen the problems myself."
Laura was so surprised that she didn't know what to say.
In the end, they shook hands.
Six months later, things were very different.
The new system had been fixed, and the team had grown to twelve people.
Customers were waiting hours instead of days for an answer.
Laura had been promoted to team leader, and she made sure that everyone in her team went home on time.
Sometimes new employees ask her about "the famous email".
Laura always laughs and tells them the whole story.
She tells them that being honest helped her more than she had expected, but that it would have been much better to say the same things politely and to the right person.
And then she gives them one piece of advice.
"Always, always check the address before you press Send."

title: The Family Restaurant
paragraphs: The restaurant was called Rossi's, and it had been standing on the corner of Station Road for almost fifty years.
It had been opened by Giorgio Rossi in 1976, when he had just arrived in England with one suitcase and his mother's recipes.
Now Giorgio was seventy-eight, and the restaurant was run by his son, Marco.
Marco's daughter, Elena, who was twenty-two, worked there at weekends while she was studying business at university.
When Elena was a child, she used to sit in the kitchen after school and watch her grandfather make pasta by hand.
The whole street would smell of garlic and fresh bread.
In those days the restaurant was always full.
People had to book a table a week in advance, and on Friday nights there was a queue outside the door.
But things had changed.
A new shopping centre had been built on the other side of town, with ten modern restaurants, bright lights and free parking.
Fewer people came to Station Road in the evenings.
Some nights, only four or five tables were taken.
The walls hadn't been painted for years, the menu was printed on old yellow paper, and the restaurant didn't even have a website.
One Sunday evening, after the last customers had left, Elena sat down at a table with her father and grandfather.
She had been thinking about this conversation for weeks.
"We need to modernise," she said.
"We need a website, online booking and a new menu with some vegetarian dishes.
And we should repaint the walls.
Everything looks so old."
Her grandfather put down his glass of wine.
"Old?" he said.
"People come here because it is old.
They come for the real taste of Italy, not for fashion."
"Grandad, nobody comes here any more," Elena replied.
"Last Tuesday we had six customers.
Six!
If we don't change something, we'll have to close within a year."
Marco rubbed his tired eyes.
He was stuck in the middle, as always.
He agreed with his daughter about the website, but he didn't want to hurt his father.
"Maybe we could make a few small changes," he suggested.
"Slowly.
Step by step."
"Small changes won't be enough," Elena said.
Giorgio stood up and walked into the kitchen without saying another word.
The conversation was over, at least for that night.
For the next two weeks, nobody mentioned the subject again.
Then, one Thursday morning, Elena was checking her phone on the bus when she saw it.
Someone had written a review of Rossi's on a popular restaurant website.
It had only one star.
The title said, "A sad place that has forgotten how to cook."
The writer complained that the soup had been cold, the waiter had been rude and the dining room had smelled of old carpet.
"This was probably a good restaurant twenty years ago," the review ended.
"Now I wouldn't recommend it to anyone.
I wish I had gone to the shopping centre instead."
Elena felt sick.
By lunchtime the review had been read by hundreds of people, and some of them had added comments.
One person wrote that they had been planning a birthday dinner at Rossi's but had changed their mind.
That evening she showed the review to her father.
Marco read it twice in silence.
Then he admitted something she hadn't known.
"The waiter was me," he said quietly.
"It was that Saturday when the chef was ill.
I had been working since six in the morning, and I was cooking and serving at the same time.
I suppose I was rude.
And the soup probably was cold."
They decided they had to show the review to Giorgio.
Elena expected him to be angry.
She thought he would say that the writer knew nothing about Italian food.
Instead, the old man read the review slowly, put on his glasses and read it again.
Then he sat for a long time without speaking.
"The carpet," he finally said.
"Is it true?
Does it smell?"
Marco and Elena looked at each other.
"A little," Marco said.
"Yes."
Giorgio nodded.
"When I opened this place, my mother told me something.
She said a restaurant is like a home.
If you invite people into your home, it must be clean and warm, and you must be happy to see them.
I think I forgot that.
I was so proud of the past that I stopped looking at the present."
He looked at his granddaughter.
"If you had shown me this a year ago, I would have been too proud to listen.
Tell me your plan."
Elena couldn't believe what she was hearing.
She ran to get her laptop.
That night the three of them stayed up until two in the morning, making a list.
They agreed to keep Giorgio's famous recipes, but to add three vegetarian dishes.
They agreed to take out the old carpet and paint the walls a warm cream colour.
Elena would build a website and look after social media.
Marco would hire an extra waiter for Saturdays, so that he wouldn't have to do two jobs at once.
The restaurant was closed for three weeks while the work was being done.
Friends and neighbours came to help.
Elena's university friends painted the walls, and an old customer who was a carpenter repaired the chairs for free.
Giorgio insisted on doing something too.
He spent every afternoon writing the new menu by hand, in beautiful old-fashioned letters, and Elena scanned it for the website.
There was one more thing that Elena wanted to do.
She found the email address of the person who had written the bad review, and she wrote them a polite message.
She thanked them for their honest opinion and explained that the restaurant was changing.
She invited them to come back for a free dinner on the opening night.
She didn't really expect an answer.
But two days later a reply arrived.
The writer, whose name was Mrs Clarke, said she was surprised.
"Most restaurants just argue with me," she wrote.
"I would be happy to come."
The opening night was a Friday in October.
Every table was full.
Elena had posted photos of the new dining room online, and lots of people had booked through the new website.
Giorgio stood at the door in his best suit, shaking hands with every guest, as he used to do many years ago.
Mrs Clarke came at eight o'clock with her husband.
She ordered the soup, of course.
Marco brought it to the table himself and apologised for her last visit.
Later, when she was leaving, she told Giorgio that the lasagne was the best she had ever eaten.
A week later, a new review appeared online.
It had five stars.
"I was wrong about Rossi's," Mrs Clarke wrote.
"Or maybe I was right, and they listened.
This family has taught me that it is never too late to change."
Now, a year later, Rossi's is busy again.
On Friday nights there is sometimes a queue outside the door.
Giorgio still comes in every afternoon to make the pasta by hand.
He has even started to enjoy reading the online reviews, and he asks Elena to read the new ones to him every morning.
"Without that terrible review," he often says, "we would have closed.
Sometimes bad news is the best thing that can happen to you."

title: The Photography Competition
paragraphs: Tom Walker had been taking photos since he was twelve, when his uncle had given him an old camera for his birthday.
Now he was thirty-four and worked as an accountant in a large office.
His job was well paid but boring, and photography was the thing that kept him happy.
Every weekend he would get up early and walk around the city with his camera, looking for interesting light, faces and streets.
He had never shown his photos to anyone except his girlfriend, Anna.
She always told him they were good enough for a gallery.
"You should do something with them," she used to say.
"They are wasted on your laptop."
One evening in March, Anna came home with a poster.
The city council was organising a photography competition called "Our City, Our Life".
Anyone could enter, and the winner would receive two thousand pounds.
The best twenty photos would be shown in an exhibition at the city museum.
"You have to enter," Anna said.
Tom laughed and shook his head.
He said that hundreds of people would take part, including professionals.
But Anna didn't give up.
She kept reminding him every day until he finally agreed to try.
The rules were simple.
Each person could send one photo, taken in the city during the last twelve months.
The deadline was the end of April.
Tom spent the next few weekends going through thousands of pictures on his laptop.
Some were nice, but none of them seemed special.
He wished he had taken more photos of people instead of buildings.
Then, three weeks before the deadline, something happened that he could never have planned.
He was waiting for a bus in the rain on a grey Monday morning.
He had his camera with him because he had been planning to take photos at lunchtime.
Suddenly, an old man walked past with a bright red umbrella.
At the same moment, a little girl in a yellow coat ran across the street to give him a flower she had picked.
The old man stopped and bent down, smiling.
Behind them, the wet street reflected the lights of the shops.
Tom didn't think.
He lifted his camera and pressed the button three times.
Then the bus arrived, and the moment was gone.
When he looked at the photos that evening, his heart started to beat faster.
The second picture was almost perfect.
The red umbrella, the yellow coat and the grey street made a beautiful picture.
You could see the surprise and happiness on the old man's face.
Anna looked at it over his shoulder and was silent for a moment.
"That's it," she said.
"That's the one."
There was just one problem.
On the left side of the photo, there was a big, ugly rubbish bin.
And above the old man's head there was an electric wire which crossed the sky.
Tom opened his editing program.
Removing the bin and the wire would only take ten minutes, and the photo would look much cleaner.
He had already started to remove the bin when he stopped.
He went back to the competition website and read the rules again, more carefully this time.
Small changes to colour and light were allowed.
But the last rule said: "Photos must show real moments.
Objects must not be added or removed."
Tom sat back in his chair.
Nobody would ever know, he thought.
The bin was not important.
It wasn't a lie, it was just a small improvement.
He asked Anna what she thought.
"It's your decision," she said.
"But if you won, would you be happy with that?"
Tom didn't answer.
He went to bed, but he couldn't sleep.
He kept thinking about his job.
Every day he checked numbers for other people, and he hated it when someone changed a small detail and hoped no one would notice.
In the end he got up at one in the morning, deleted the edited version and sent the original.
He only made the colours a little brighter, which the rules allowed.
In the form, he gave the photo a title: "A Flower in the Rain".
Five weeks later, he received an email.
His photo had been chosen as one of the twenty finalists.
The photos would be shown at the museum, and the winner would be announced on the opening night.
Tom read the email four times before he believed it.
The opening night was in June.
The museum was full of people in smart clothes, drinking wine and talking.
Tom felt nervous and out of place.
He walked around and looked at the other photos.
Many of them were amazing: perfect sunsets, perfect bridges, perfect faces.
Some of them were so perfect that they looked almost unreal.
Then the head of the jury, a well-known photographer called Mrs Hughes, stood up to speak.
She thanked everyone and then said something that surprised the room.
"This year we received more than eight hundred photos," she said.
"Sadly, we had to remove eleven of them from the competition, including two which had been chosen as finalists.
We discovered that objects had been removed or added in an editing program.
Some of these photos were very beautiful.
But a beautiful photo is not always a true photo."
Tom felt his face go hot.
He thought about the rubbish bin.
If he had removed it, his photo might have been one of the eleven.
"Our winner," Mrs Hughes went on, "is a photo that shows our city exactly as it is.
It is not perfect.
There is a rubbish bin in it, and there is a wire across the sky.
But it shows a real moment of kindness between two strangers, and that is what this city is about.
The winner is Tom Walker, for 'A Flower in the Rain'."
At first Tom didn't move.
Anna had to push him gently towards the stage.
He shook hands with Mrs Hughes, and everyone clapped.
Later, she told him that the jury had studied his photo very carefully.
"The bin actually helped," she said with a smile.
"It proved to us that you hadn't touched anything."
There was one more surprise that evening.
While Tom was talking to a journalist, an old man came up to him with a little girl.
It was the man with the red umbrella.
His granddaughter had seen the photo in the newspaper, and they had come to the museum to see it.
The old man told Tom that his wife had died the year before.
That morning, he explained, had been the first time he had smiled for months.
Tom used part of the prize money to buy a better camera.
He printed a large copy of the photo and gave it to the old man and his granddaughter.
He still works as an accountant, but now he teaches a photography class for beginners on Saturday mornings.
On the first day of every course, he tells his students the same thing.
"Don't try to make the world perfect," he says.
"Try to see it honestly.
That is much more difficult, and much more interesting."

title: The Online Scam
paragraphs: Harold Green was eighty-one years old, and he had lived alone since his wife, Mary, had died four years earlier.
He lived in a small house with a garden full of roses, which Mary had planted many years before.
Harold had worked as a train driver for forty years.
He was careful with money, and over his long life he had saved nearly thirty thousand pounds.
He used to say that this money was for his granddaughter, Lucy, and for "a rainy day".
Lucy was twenty-five and worked as a nurse in a hospital across town.
She visited her grandfather every Sunday.
Two years earlier, she had bought him a tablet and taught him how to use it.
At first Harold had refused to touch it.
But slowly he had started to enjoy it.
He read the news, looked at photos of trains and sent Lucy short messages with too many full stops.
One Tuesday afternoon, the phone rang.
A polite young man introduced himself as Daniel from the fraud department of Harold's bank.
He knew Harold's full name and address, and he even knew the name of his bank.
"I'm afraid there is a problem, Mr Green," he said.
"Someone has been trying to take money from your account.
We think criminals have stolen your details."
Harold felt his stomach go cold.
He asked what he should do.
Daniel explained that the bank needed to move his money to a new, safe account as quickly as possible.
"Don't worry," he said in a calm voice.
"We do this every day.
I'll help you step by step."
Daniel told Harold to open his tablet and download a small program.
He said it would allow the bank to "check the computer for viruses".
Harold did what he was told.
Then Daniel asked him to open his online banking.
"Please don't tell anyone about this call," Daniel added.
"The criminals may be watching.
Even your family might be in danger if they know."
For the next hour, Daniel guided him through everything.
Harold had to read out a code that had been sent to his phone.
Daniel said this was a normal security check.
Then a message appeared on the screen.
It said that ten thousand pounds would be transferred to the new account.
Harold hesitated.
"Ten thousand?" he asked.
"Is that right?"
"That's only the first part," Daniel said.
"We'll move the rest tomorrow.
You're doing very well, Mr Green."
Harold's hand was shaking.
Something didn't feel right, but Daniel sounded so kind and so professional.
He was just about to press the button when he heard a knock at the door.
It was his neighbour, Mrs Patel, who had brought him some soup.
Harold told Daniel he would call him back, and he put the phone down.
Mrs Patel noticed immediately that he looked pale.
When she asked what was wrong, Harold remembered that he had promised not to tell anyone.
But he was too worried to keep quiet.
He told her everything.
Mrs Patel listened and then said firmly, "Harold, call Lucy.
Right now."
Lucy was on her break at the hospital when her phone rang.
As soon as she heard the words "safe account", she knew.
"Grandad, don't press anything," she said.
"Turn the tablet off.
That man wasn't from the bank.
It's a scam."
She left work early and drove straight to his house.
Harold was sitting at the kitchen table, looking much older than usual.
Lucy called the real bank using the number on the back of his card.
The woman she spoke to confirmed that the bank had never called him.
She explained that a bank would never ask a customer to move money to another account, and it would never ask for security codes on the phone.
Harold's account was blocked for a few days to protect it, and his money was safe.
Not a single pound had been lost.
But Harold didn't feel lucky.
He felt stupid and ashamed.
"I drove trains for forty years," he said quietly.
"Thousands of people trusted me with their lives.
And I nearly gave all my money to a stranger on the phone.
If Mrs Patel hadn't knocked on the door, I would have lost everything.
How could I be so foolish?"
Lucy held his hand.
She told him that these criminals were very clever.
They had stolen information from somewhere, so they had sounded real.
"They don't only call old people," she said.
"Last year a doctor I work with lost five thousand pounds in the same way.
She's thirty-five and very smart.
These people are professionals.
You did nothing wrong by believing them.
You did the right thing by stopping."
They reported the call to the police.
A young police officer came the next day and asked Harold a lot of questions.
She asked him what the man had sounded like and whether he had given his real name.
She also asked how much information the caller had known.
Then she told them something surprising.
In the past month, more than forty similar calls had been reported in their part of town.
Most of the victims were over seventy, and many of them had been too embarrassed to tell their families.
That evening, Lucy found her grandfather sitting quietly at the table.
"Forty people," he said.
"I wish someone had warned me.
If I had known how these people work, I would have put the phone down at once."
Then he looked up at her.
"Maybe we could warn the others."
It was his idea, but Lucy helped to organise it.
They asked the manager of the local community centre if they could use a room.
Lucy designed a simple poster on her computer, and Harold put copies in the library, the post office and the chemist's.
The poster said: "Has someone called you about your money?
Come and talk.
Free tea and biscuits."
On the first Thursday, Lucy expected five or six people.
Thirty-two people came.
Harold stood at the front, nervous at first, and told his story honestly.
He didn't hide how close he had come to losing his savings.
When he finished, the room was quiet.
Then an old woman in the second row put her hand up.
She said the same thing had happened to her husband, but he had never told anyone because he felt so ashamed.
One by one, other people began to share their stories.
Lucy then explained a few simple rules.
Never give security codes to anyone.
Never download a program because a stranger tells you to.
If someone says your money is in danger, put the phone down and call your bank yourself, using a number you trust.
And if someone tells you to keep a secret from your family, that is the clearest warning of all.
The meetings became a regular event, on the first Thursday of every month.
A local newspaper wrote an article about them, with a photo of Harold holding a cup of tea.
The headline was "Former Train Driver Helps Neighbours Stay on the Right Track".
Harold pretended to be embarrassed, but Lucy noticed that he had cut out the article and put it on the fridge.
Now, whenever Harold's phone rings and he doesn't know the number, he smiles and says, "Sorry, I never discuss money on the phone.
Goodbye."
Then he sends Lucy a message, with far too many full stops, to tell her that another one has tried and failed.

title: The Flat Share
paragraphs: When Maya moved to London for her first job, she couldn't afford to rent a flat on her own.
Prices were much higher than she had expected.
After three weeks of searching, she found a room in a big old flat above a bakery in the north of the city.
Three other people already lived there, and the rent was cheap.
The advert had said, "Friendly, quiet flat.
Looking for a fourth person."
Maya would soon discover that only half of this was true.
The other three people couldn't have been more different.
Greg was a forty-year-old taxi driver who had lived in the flat for eight years.
He worked at night, slept during the day, and was very serious about rules.
Sofia was a music student from Brazil who practised the violin for hours every day.
And Kevin was a computer programmer who almost never left his room, except to cook strange meals at two o'clock in the morning.
On her first evening, Greg gave Maya a piece of paper with a list on it.
It was titled "Flat Rules" and it had twenty-three points.
Nobody was allowed to use the washing machine after nine in the evening.
Shoes had to be taken off at the door.
Food in the fridge had to be labelled with your name.
Maya laughed, thinking it was a joke.
Greg didn't laugh.
At first, Maya tried hard to follow all the rules.
But it was difficult to live with people who had such different lives.
Greg needed silence during the day, but that was exactly when Sofia wanted to practise.
Kevin's cooking filled the flat with the smell of fish and burnt onions at night.
Sofia never washed her dishes, and they were often left in the sink for days.
Kevin borrowed things without asking.
Maya found herself in the middle of every argument.
The worst argument happened in November.
Greg had come home after a long night shift and found that someone had eaten his cheese, which had been clearly labelled.
He knocked loudly on every door and called a "flat meeting" in the kitchen.
"I'm tired of this," he said.
"I've lived here for eight years, and I've never had such terrible flatmates."
Sofia said that his rules were crazy and that the flat felt like a prison.
Kevin said nothing at all and stared at his phone.
Maya tried to calm everyone down.
In the end, Sofia went to her room and slammed the door, and Greg went to bed.
Maya sat alone in the kitchen.
She remembered how excited she had been when she arrived.
Now she wished she had chosen a different flat.
If she had known it would be like this, she would have paid more to live alone.
For the next few weeks, the flatmates barely spoke to each other.
They put notes on the fridge instead.
"Who left the light on?"
"Please stop playing music at 8 o'clock."
"Whose socks are these?"
Maya started to look at adverts for other rooms.
She had even arranged to see one on the following Saturday.
Then, on a freezing night in December, everything changed.
Maya woke up at three in the morning because she was cold.
She went to the kitchen and noticed a strange smell.
At first she thought it was Kevin's cooking again, but this smell was different.
It was smoke.
It was coming from under the floor, from the bakery downstairs.
She ran from door to door, shouting.
Kevin opened his door immediately; he had been awake, as usual.
Sofia came out in her pyjamas, confused and half asleep.
"Where's Greg?" Maya asked.
Then she remembered that Greg was working that night.
Kevin called the fire service while Maya and Sofia grabbed their coats.
The smoke was getting thicker.
They were about to leave when Sofia stopped.
"My violin," she said.
It had belonged to her grandfather, and it was the only one she had.
Before anyone could stop her, she ran back to her room.
Maya was terrified.
Kevin went after Sofia, and a few seconds later they both came back, coughing, with the violin case.
The three of them ran down the stairs and out into the cold street.
The fire engines arrived within five minutes.
The firefighters told them later that an electric oven had been left on in the bakery.
The fire had been burning slowly for an hour before Maya noticed the smell.
"If you hadn't woken up," a firefighter said to her, "this could have been much worse."
They stood on the pavement in the freezing wind for a long time.
Sofia was shaking, and Kevin gave her his jacket.
At about four o'clock, a taxi stopped in front of the building.
It was Greg.
Kevin had called him, and he had driven straight home.
When he saw them, he jumped out of the car and ran towards them.
"Is everyone all right?" he kept asking.
Maya had never seen him look so worried.
Greg made them all get into his taxi to keep warm.
He turned on the heating and gave them a bag of biscuits he had been keeping for his break.
For a while nobody said anything.
Then Kevin said quietly, "I ate your cheese.
In November.
I'm sorry."
There was a short silence.
Then Greg started laughing, and soon all four of them were laughing so much that they could hardly breathe.
Luckily, the fire had not reached the flat.
Only the bakery kitchen had been damaged.
But the flat smelled of smoke, so the four of them had to stay somewhere else for a week.
Greg's sister, who had a big house outside the city, invited them all to stay with her.
That week was the first time they had really talked to each other.
Maya learned that Greg had been strict about rules because his wife had left him eight years ago, and the flat was the only thing he still felt in control of.
Kevin admitted that he had been very lonely since moving from Scotland, and that he cooked at night because he couldn't sleep.
Sofia explained that she practised so much because her family had sold their car to pay for her studies.
She was afraid of letting them down.
When they moved back into the flat, things were different.
They sat down together and wrote new rules.
This time there were only five.
Sofia would practise in the afternoon, when Greg was already awake.
Kevin would open the window when he cooked.
Everyone would wash their own dishes.
Nobody would eat Greg's cheese.
And every Sunday evening they would have dinner together.
Maya cancelled her appointment to see the other room.
A year later, she still lives in the flat above the bakery.
The Sunday dinners have become the best part of her week.
Each person takes a turn to cook, and Sofia usually plays the violin afterwards.
Even Greg, who used to complain about the noise, asks her for his favourite song.
Sometimes Maya thinks about the advert that brought her there.
"Friendly, quiet flat."
It still isn't quiet.
But now, at last, it is friendly.

title: The Last Train Home
paragraphs: Clare had been waiting for this concert for six months.
Her favourite band, who hadn't played together for ten years, had announced a short tour, and the closest concert was in a city two hours away by train.
She had bought the ticket on the first day, even though it was expensive.
Her friend Jess had promised to come with her, but she had cancelled at the last minute because she was ill.
So Clare decided to go alone.
She had checked the timetable carefully before she left.
The last train home left at twenty past eleven.
The concert was supposed to finish at half past ten, so she would have plenty of time.
She had to be at work at nine the next morning, and she couldn't afford to miss that train.
The concert was even better than she had hoped.
The band played all their old songs, and the crowd sang every word.
Clare sang and danced until her voice was almost gone.
But the band kept coming back for one more song, and then another.
When the lights finally came on, it was ten past eleven.
Clare ran out of the hall and through the wet streets.
Her phone said the station was twelve minutes away on foot.
She ran the whole way, pushing past people and nearly falling twice.
When she reached the platform, out of breath, she saw the red lights of the train disappearing into the dark.
She had missed it by less than a minute.
For a moment she just stood there.
Then she went to the ticket office, but it was closed.
An old man who was cleaning the floor told her there were no more trains to her town until six in the morning.
"But there's a night bus," he said kindly.
"It doesn't go all the way, but it goes halfway, to a little town called Ashford.
From there you can catch the first train at half past five."
Clare didn't want to stay in the big city alone, and the hotels near the station looked expensive.
So she took the night bus.
She was the only passenger.
The driver, a large man with a grey beard, asked her where she was going.
When she explained what had happened, he shook his head.
"You'll have a long wait in Ashford," he said.
"There's nothing there at night.
The station closes at midnight."
The bus stopped in Ashford at a quarter to one.
The driver had been right.
The little town was completely dark and silent.
The station was locked, and the only light came from a street lamp.
It was cold, and it had started to rain again.
Clare's phone battery was at four percent.
She wished she had brought a charger.
If only Jess hadn't been ill, she thought, at least she wouldn't be alone.
She walked along the main street, looking for anywhere that was still open.
Everything was closed: the café, the chemist's, the pub.
Then, at the end of the street, she noticed a light in a window.
It was a small shop whose sign said "Books and Records".
Through the window she could see an old woman sitting in an armchair, reading.
Clare hesitated.
It was almost one o'clock in the morning, and she didn't want to frighten anyone.
But the rain was getting heavier.
She knocked gently on the glass.
The woman looked up, surprised, and then came to the door.
"I'm so sorry to bother you," Clare said.
She explained about the concert, the train and the bus.
The woman listened, and then she smiled.
"Come in, dear, before you catch a cold," she said.
"I'm Margaret.
I never sleep much anyway."
The shop was warm and full of old books and records.
It smelled of paper and coffee.
Margaret made two cups of hot chocolate and found a charger for Clare's phone.
She asked Clare which band she had seen.
When Clare told her, Margaret's eyes lit up.
She went to a shelf and came back with an old record.
It was the band's first album, signed by all four members.
"How did you get this?" Clare asked, amazed.
Margaret laughed.
She explained that thirty years ago, before they were famous, the band had played in the pub across the street.
After the concert, their van had broken down, and they had been stuck in Ashford for the night.
"My husband and I used to run this shop together," she said.
"He invited them in, just like I invited you.
They sat right where you're sitting and played their guitars until morning.
In the morning they signed this for us to say thank you."
Clare could hardly believe it.
She told Margaret that the singer had mentioned a small town at the concert.
He had said that a stranger's kindness in a little town had once saved the band.
He had said that the first song they ever wrote had been written that night.
"He didn't say the name of the town," Clare said.
"But it must have been here."
Margaret was quiet for a moment.
Her husband, she explained, had died two years earlier.
Since then, the shop had been struggling.
Not many people bought records any more, and she was thinking of closing it.
"Sometimes I wonder whether anyone remembers this place," she said.
They talked for hours.
Margaret told Clare about her husband, who had loved music more than anything.
Clare told Margaret about her job in an office, which she didn't enjoy, and about how she used to play the piano before she stopped having time for it.
Margaret asked her why she had given it up.
Clare couldn't really answer.
At some point Margaret played a few records, and they listened in silence while the rain fell outside.
At five o'clock, Margaret walked her to the station.
The sky was getting lighter, and the birds had started singing.
Before the train came, Clare asked if she could take a photo of the signed record and of the shop.
Margaret agreed, a little confused.
On the train, Clare wrote a long post about her night.
She described how she had missed the last train and how she had been welcomed by a stranger in a little shop full of records.
She explained the story of the band and the signed album.
Finally, she added the photos and the name of the shop.
She tagged the band's official page, not really expecting anything to happen.
Then she fell asleep with her head against the window.
When she woke up, her phone was full of notifications.
Her post had been shared thousands of times.
Fans from all over the country were asking for the address of the shop.
And that afternoon, the band's singer wrote a reply.
He said they had been looking for that shop for years, but they had forgotten the name of the town.
Two months later, the band played a small free concert in the pub across the street from Margaret's shop.
The town had never been so busy.
People came from far away, and almost every one of them visited "Books and Records".
Margaret sold more records in one weekend than she had sold in the previous year.
Clare was there, of course, standing at the front with Jess.
After the concert, Margaret gave her a small package.
Inside was a piano book and a note.
It said, "For the girl who missed the train.
Don't wait too long to play again."
Clare has started taking piano lessons since then.
And every time she goes to a concert now, she checks the timetable twice.
But secretly, she is very glad that once, she didn't.
