title: The Language Exchange
paragraphs: When Dmitry arrived in London, he thought his English was good.
He had studied it at school and at university in Yekaterinburg, and for five years he had read technical documents in English almost every day.
He was an engineer, and he had been offered a job with a company which designed bridges.
On paper, everything was perfect.
The problem was that real people did not speak like technical documents.
In his first week, a colleague asked him, "Fancy a cuppa?"
Dmitry smiled politely and said nothing, because he had no idea what the question meant.
Later he found out that it was simply an offer of a cup of tea.
He wished he had asked.
After a month, he realised that he needed to practise speaking with someone who would not laugh at his mistakes.
One evening, in the local library, he noticed a small piece of paper on the noticeboard.
It said: "Student of Russian looking for a native speaker for a language exchange.
One hour English, one hour Russian.
Free coffee included!"
There was a phone number and a name: Emma.
Dmitry used to be quite shy, and in Russia he would never have called a stranger.
But London had already changed him a little.
He sent a message, and two days later he was sitting in a café near the library, opposite a young woman with red hair and a big smile.
Emma was twenty, and she was studying Russian and French at university.
She had fallen in love with Russian literature after reading a book by Chekhov at school.
"I can read quite well," she explained, "but when I try to speak, my brain stops working.
Last summer I went to Saint Petersburg for two weeks, and I was too scared to say anything except 'thank you'."
They agreed to meet every Thursday at six.
For the first hour they would speak English, and Emma would correct Dmitry.
For the second hour they would switch to Russian, and Dmitry would help her.
The first meetings were full of misunderstandings.
Once Emma told him that his presentation idea was "quite good".
Dmitry felt happy until she explained that, in British English, "quite good" often means "not very good".
He was shocked.
"So when my manager says my work is quite interesting, he doesn't like it?" Emma laughed.
"It depends on his voice," she said.
"English people rarely say what they really mean."
Emma had her own problems too.
She told Dmitry that she had once tried to buy bread in a Russian shop and had used the polite form of "you" with a cat.
Another time she had wanted to say that she was tired, but the word she used meant that she was bored with the person in front of her.
"No wonder the man looked offended," she said, covering her face with her hands.
They also talked about culture.
Emma asked him why Russians didn't smile at strangers in the street.
Dmitry explained that in Russia a smile was something you gave to people you knew.
"If you smile at a stranger for no reason, people think something is wrong with you," he said.
Emma found this fascinating.
In return, she explained why British people apologised all the time, even when someone else had stepped on their foot.
Week after week, the conversations became easier.
Dmitry started to understand jokes at work, and he even made one himself during a meeting.
Everyone laughed, and he wasn't sure if they were laughing at the joke or at him, but it still felt like a victory.
Emma, meanwhile, had stopped translating every sentence in her head before she spoke.
Then, in March, something went wrong.
One Thursday, Dmitry waited at the café for forty minutes, but Emma didn't come.
She didn't answer his messages either.
The next week, the same thing happened.
Dmitry felt hurt.
He decided that their friendship had only been a polite arrangement for her, and that she had simply lost interest.
"If I had known that she would disappear like this," he thought, "I wouldn't have spent so much time preparing for our meetings."
Three weeks later, he received a long message.
Emma's grandmother had been taken to hospital after a fall, and Emma had gone home to Leeds to look after her.
She had lost her phone on the train and had only just bought a new one.
"I'm so sorry," she wrote.
"I should have found a way to tell you.
Are you still free on Thursdays?"
Dmitry felt ashamed.
He had judged her too quickly.
He wrote back immediately and asked how her grandmother was.
Emma said that she was getting better, but slowly.
When they met again, Emma looked worried.
Her oral exam in Russian was in two weeks, and she had missed a lot of classes.
The examiner would ask her to speak for ten minutes about a topic and then answer questions.
"I'm going to fail," she said.
"I've forgotten everything."
Dmitry suggested meeting twice a week instead of once until the exam.
They practised for hours.
He pretended to be a strict examiner, asking difficult questions about Russian history, food and family traditions.
When she made mistakes, he wrote them down and they went through them together at the end.
He told her that she should stop apologising for every small error.
"Russians will understand you," he said.
"They are just happy that you are trying."
At the same time, Dmitry had his own challenge.
His team was preparing a presentation for an important client, and his manager had asked him to present the technical part.
Dmitry had never spoken in front of a large group in English.
So Emma helped him in return.
She listened to his presentation again and again, and she showed him how to make his sentences shorter and more natural.
"Don't say 'it is necessary to underline the fact that'," she told him.
"Just say 'the important thing is'."
The presentation was on a Tuesday, and Emma's exam was on the Wednesday.
On Tuesday evening, Dmitry sent her a message: "The client asked me three questions and I understood all of them.
My manager said my part was 'really excellent'.
Not 'quite good'!"
Emma replied with ten smiling faces.
On Wednesday afternoon, Dmitry's phone rang during a meeting.
He went out into the corridor to answer it.
Emma was shouting so loudly that he had to hold the phone away from his ear.
She had passed with one of the highest marks in her year.
The examiner had told her that her Russian sounded natural and confident.
He had even asked her whether she had lived in Russia.
That Thursday, they met at the café as usual, but this time Emma brought a cake.
She had baked it herself, using a recipe from Dmitry's grandmother, which he had translated for her.
It wasn't perfect, but Dmitry said it was the best cake he had eaten in London.
"You know," Emma said, "when I put that note on the noticeboard, I only wanted to improve my Russian.
I didn't expect to find a friend."
Dmitry smiled, and for once he didn't care whether it was the Russian or the British way of smiling.
"Neither did I," he said.
"Same time next week?"
"Of course," she answered in Russian, without even thinking about it.

title: The Broken Promise
paragraphs: Mark Turner had always believed that he was a good father.
He worked hard, he paid for everything his family needed, and every summer he took them on holiday to Spain.
His son, Leo, was nine, and Mark loved him more than anything in the world.
The problem was that he rarely had time to show it.
Mark was a manager at a large insurance company in Manchester.
Two years earlier, he had been promoted, and since then his working day had become longer and longer.
He usually left the house before Leo woke up and came home after Leo had gone to bed.
At weekends his phone never stopped ringing.
Even at dinner, he would check his emails under the table, while his wife, Helen, looked at him without saying anything.
It hadn't always been like this.
When Leo was small, Mark used to take him to the park every Saturday morning.
They would feed the ducks, play football and then buy hot chocolate from a little van near the gate.
Leo still talked about those mornings, but they seemed like a long time ago now.
In the past year, Mark had missed a lot of important moments.
He had missed Leo's first swimming competition because of a meeting with a client.
He had missed parents' evening at school because his train had been cancelled on the way back from London.
He had even arrived late for Leo's birthday party, when all the cake had already been eaten.
Each time, he apologised and promised that it would never happen again.
Each time, Leo said, "It's OK, Dad."
But Mark noticed that he said it more quietly every time.
One evening in October, Leo was still awake when Mark came home.
He was sitting on the stairs in his pyjamas, holding a piece of paper.
"Dad, I've been given a part in the school play," he said proudly.
"I'm the king!
It's on the twelfth of December at six o'clock.
Will you come?"
Mark took the paper and read it.
"Of course I'll come," he said.
"I promise.
I wouldn't miss it for anything."
"You promised last time too," Leo said.
Then he went upstairs before Mark could answer.
Those words stayed in Mark's head all night.
He wrote the date in his diary, in his phone and on the calendar in the kitchen.
He told his secretary that he must not be disturbed on the afternoon of the twelfth.
He even asked Helen to remind him every week.
For the next two months, Leo practised his lines every evening with his mother.
Sometimes, when Mark came home early enough, he could hear Leo's voice from the living room: "I am the king of this land, and I will not be afraid!"
Mark would stand in the corridor and listen with a smile, but he never went in, because he always had another phone call to make.
On the morning of the twelfth, Mark woke up with a good feeling.
He had planned everything.
He would leave the office at four, which would give him plenty of time to drive to the school.
But at eleven o'clock, his boss, Mr Graham, called him into his office.
"We have a serious problem," Mr Graham said.
"Our biggest client wants to cancel their contract.
Their director is flying in from Germany this afternoon.
I need you at the meeting.
It starts at three and it might go on until late."
Mark felt his stomach turn.
He explained that his son's school play was that evening and that he had promised to be there.
Mr Graham looked at him in surprise.
He asked Mark whether he really understood how important this client was.
"If we lose this contract," he said, "people could lose their jobs.
Maybe even you."
Mark went back to his desk and sat there for a long time.
He thought about all the times he had chosen work over his family.
He remembered Leo's face on the stairs.
If only he hadn't made so many promises that he couldn't keep.
He picked up his phone to send Helen a message, saying that he would be late again.
He typed it, read it, and then deleted it.
Then he did something he had never done before.
He went back to Mr Graham's office and knocked on the door.
"I'm sorry," he said.
"I'll prepare everything for the meeting, and Sarah from my team can present it.
She knows the client as well as I do.
But I'm leaving at four.
My son has been waiting for this evening for two months.
If I break this promise, I don't think he'll ever believe me again."
Mr Graham was silent for a moment.
Mark was sure that he was going to be shouted at.
Instead, his boss sighed and looked at a photo on his desk.
It showed two teenage girls on a beach.
"My daughters are at university now," he said quietly.
"I can't remember a single one of their school plays.
I wasn't there for any of them."
He told Mark to go.
Mark spent the next four hours working harder than he had ever worked.
He wrote notes for Sarah, prepared all the documents and called the client to apologise personally.
At five past four, he ran out of the building.
The traffic was terrible.
It was raining heavily, and there had been an accident on the main road.
Mark sat in his car, watching the minutes pass.
At ten to six, he was still three kilometres from the school.
He left the car in a supermarket car park and ran the rest of the way in the rain, in his expensive office shoes.
When he opened the door of the school hall, the lights had already been turned off and the play had started.
He was completely wet, and his hair was stuck to his forehead.
He stood at the back, trying to breathe quietly.
A few minutes later, the king came onto the stage.
Leo was wearing a golden paper crown and a red cloak which Helen had made from an old curtain.
He looked out at the audience, searching for something.
Mark knew exactly what he was looking for.
He raised his hand and waved.
Leo saw him.
For a second he forgot his line, and then the biggest smile Mark had ever seen spread across his face.
"I am the king of this land," Leo said, louder and more confidently than ever, "and I will not be afraid!"
After the play, Leo ran across the hall and jumped into his father's arms, even though Mark was still wet.
"You came!" he shouted.
"You really came!"
"I promised," Mark said, and his voice was not quite steady.
The next day, he found out that Sarah's presentation had gone very well and that the client had decided to stay.
Nobody lost their job.
Mark realised that the company had survived one afternoon without him, and that perhaps it could survive more.
From then on, things changed.
Mark stopped checking his emails at dinner, and he turned his phone off at weekends.
He started leaving work at five on Fridays.
And on Saturday mornings, if the weather wasn't too bad, he and Leo went to the park again to feed the ducks and buy hot chocolate from the little van near the gate.

title: The Charity Concert
paragraphs: The Sunflower Children's Centre had been open for almost thirty years.
It was a small building with a yellow door, at the end of a quiet street in Bristol, where children from poor families could come after school.
They did their homework there, played games, ate a hot meal and talked to adults who listened to them.
For many of them, it was the safest place they knew.
Anna Clarke worked in the accounts department of a large travel company nearby.
She had a special reason to care about the centre.
When she was a child, she had gone there every afternoon, because her mother worked late and there was nobody at home.
The woman who ran it, Mrs Patel, had helped her with her maths and had taught her to believe in herself.
One Monday in April, Anna read in the local newspaper that the centre was going to be closed.
The council had cut its budget, and the building needed a new roof, which would cost twelve thousand pounds.
If the money wasn't found by the end of June, the doors would be locked for good.
That lunchtime, Anna told her colleagues about it.
"I wish I could do something," she said.
"But I don't have twelve thousand pounds."
"None of us do," said Tom from IT.
"But together we could raise it."
Tom played the guitar in a band at weekends.
He suggested organising a charity concert.
Everyone thought it was a brilliant idea.
Grace from marketing offered to design the posters.
Raj, who was good with numbers, agreed to deal with the tickets.
Anna was chosen to be in charge of everything.
At first, everything went smoothly.
Anna phoned the manager of the town hall, who agreed to let them use the main hall for free on the last Saturday in June.
Tom's band agreed to play, and so did a choir from a local church and a young singer called Mia, who had become famous after appearing on a television talent show.
Grace's posters were put up all over the town.
Within two weeks, three hundred tickets had been sold.
Then the problems started.
First, the town hall called.
A pipe had burst in the main hall, and the floor had been badly damaged.
It would be repaired, but not before July.
Anna spent three days phoning every possible place in the town.
In the end, the head teacher of a secondary school agreed to let them use the school sports hall.
It wasn't beautiful, but it was big enough.
A week later, Mia's manager sent an email.
He said that Mia had been offered a performance at a festival in London on the same night, and that she was very sorry, but she couldn't come.
Anna read the email twice and then put her head on her desk.
Many people had bought tickets only because they wanted to see Mia.
"If I had signed a contract with her," she said to Tom, "she couldn't have done this."
"It isn't your fault," Tom told her.
"Let's think about who else could play."
The worst moment came ten days before the concert.
Raj came into the office looking pale.
He explained that the website they had used for the tickets had made a mistake.
Instead of three hundred tickets, it had sold four hundred and fifty, but the sports hall could only hold four hundred people.
Anna felt like crying.
She asked Raj how something like that could have happened.
He said he had no idea, but that the company had promised to give refunds to anyone who wanted one.
That evening, Anna went to the children's centre.
She had been working on the concert for two months, and she was exhausted.
She told Mrs Patel, who was now in her seventies, that she was thinking of giving up.
"Maybe it was a stupid idea," she said.
"Everything is going wrong."
Mrs Patel took her hand.
"Do you remember when you were ten and you failed your maths test?" she asked.
"You told me you would never understand fractions.
Two weeks later, you got the highest mark in your class.
You have never been someone who gives up, Anna."
Then a small boy called Jayden, who had been listening, pulled Anna's sleeve.
"We could sing," he said.
"We've been practising a song for the summer party."
Anna looked at him, and suddenly she had an idea.
Instead of a famous singer, the children from the centre would perform.
The audience would see exactly who they were helping.
And for the extra people, they could open the doors at the back of the hall and put chairs in the playground outside, where speakers would be set up.
The day of the concert arrived.
Of course, more things went wrong.
Tom's car broke down on the way, and he had to come by bus with his guitar.
The church choir got lost and arrived forty minutes late.
At four o'clock, it started to rain, and the chairs in the playground had to be covered with plastic sheets.
Anna ran from one problem to another, and she didn't stop to eat or drink all afternoon.
But at seven o'clock, the sports hall was full.
People were standing along the walls and sitting on the floor.
Outside, under umbrellas, another hundred people were waiting to listen.
The choir sang first, and then Tom's band played for an hour.
People were dancing between the chairs.
Finally, Anna went onto the stage and explained why they were all there.
She told them about the yellow door and about the woman who had helped a lonely little girl with her maths.
Her voice was shaking, but she managed to finish.
Then twenty children walked onto the stage, holding hands.
Jayden stood at the front.
They sang a simple song about friendship, a little out of tune, and some of them forgot the words.
By the end, half of the audience was in tears.
When the song finished, everyone stood up and clapped for almost five minutes.
After the concert, Raj counted the money.
With the tickets, the donations and the cakes that had been sold at the door, they had raised nine thousand four hundred pounds.
It was a fantastic result, but it wasn't enough.
Anna tried to smile, but she was disappointed.
Almost three thousand pounds were still missing.
On Monday morning, a man in a grey suit came into the office and asked for Anna.
He introduced himself as the owner of a local building company.
He had been sitting in the playground on Saturday, under an umbrella, and he had listened to the children singing.
"I went to that centre too, when I was a boy," he said.
"My company will repair the roof.
You won't have to pay for the work, only for the materials."
The roof was finished at the end of July.
The Sunflower Children's Centre didn't close, and the money which remained was used to buy new books and computers.
Anna, Tom, Grace and Raj had learned a lot from the experience.
Organising a concert was much harder than they had imagined, and almost nothing had gone according to plan.
But when Anna walked past the yellow door now and heard children laughing inside, she knew that every difficult moment had been worth it.
In fact, they were already talking about next year's concert.

title: Working from Home
paragraphs: For six years, Lucy Morgan had travelled to work every day by train.
She was a graphic designer in a busy agency in the centre of London, and the journey took an hour and a quarter each way.
She spent those hours standing in crowded carriages, with someone's elbow in her back and someone else's coffee too close to her shirt.
Every evening, she arrived home tired and hungry, with no energy left for anything else.
So when her boss, Karen, announced that the agency was going to let some designers work from home permanently, Lucy was the first to put her hand up.
"Are you sure?" Karen asked.
"Some people find it harder than they expect." Lucy laughed.
She couldn't imagine anything better than never having to take that train again.
The first few weeks were wonderful.
Lucy turned the small spare room in her flat into an office.
She bought a large desk, a comfortable chair and a plant, which she put next to the window.
She no longer had to get up at six.
Instead, she woke up at half past seven, made herself a proper breakfast and started work at half past eight, still wearing her slippers.
She loved the silence.
In the agency, there had always been phones ringing and people chatting, and she had found it difficult to concentrate.
At home, she could listen to her own music and work without being interrupted.
She finished her projects faster than ever.
At lunchtime, she went for a walk in the park near her flat, and in the evenings she had time to cook, read and see her friends.
"Why didn't I do this years ago?" she asked herself.
But slowly, without noticing it, things began to change.
It started with small habits.
One morning, she decided that there was no point in getting dressed, since nobody would see her.
She worked all day in her pyjamas.
A few days later, she stopped making breakfast and just ate a biscuit at her desk.
The lunchtime walks became shorter, and then they stopped completely, because it was easier to eat a sandwich in front of the computer.
Her working day also became longer.
In the office, she had always left at half past five, when everyone else left.
At home, there was nobody to tell her when the day was over.
Her laptop was always in the next room, and she would often go back "just to check one thing" at nine or ten in the evening.
Soon she was answering emails in bed.
Her friends invited her out, but she usually said she was too busy.
By the end of the winter, Lucy had stopped looking forward to anything.
Some days she didn't speak to a single person except the delivery driver who brought her shopping.
She had been working from home for five months, and she couldn't remember the last time she had laughed out loud.
She missed the stupid jokes in the office kitchen.
She even missed her colleague Ben, who used to sing badly while he worked and who had driven her crazy.
Her work suffered too.
She had always been proud of her ideas, but now they seemed boring and tired.
In a video meeting in February, Karen asked her why her latest designs looked so similar to her old ones.
Lucy didn't know what to say.
After the meeting, she sat at her desk for a long time without moving.
The turning point came on a grey Sunday in March.
Lucy's sister, Kate, came to visit without warning.
When Lucy opened the door, Kate stared at her.
Lucy was wearing the same old jumper she had been wearing for three days, and there were dirty cups on every surface of the flat.
The plant by the window had died weeks ago, and Lucy hadn't even noticed.
"Lucy, what's happened to you?" Kate asked.
"You look terrible.
When was the last time you went outside?"
Lucy started to answer, but then, to her own surprise, she burst into tears.
She told Kate everything: the loneliness, the long hours, the feeling that her days had no beginning and no end.
"I thought I would be so happy," she said.
"I wish I had listened to Karen.
She warned me that it might be difficult."
Kate made them both a cup of tea and sat down next to her.
"Working from home isn't the problem," she said.
"The problem is that you've stopped looking after yourself.
You need some rules."
They spent the rest of the afternoon writing a plan.
Kate, who had worked from home for years as a translator, explained the things that had helped her.
That evening, Lucy stuck the list on the wall above her desk.
The rules were simple.
She had to get up at the same time every day and get dressed as if she were going to the office.
She had to start work at nine and stop at half past five, and after that the door of the spare room had to be closed.
She was not allowed to eat lunch at her desk.
She had to go outside at least once a day, even if it was raining.
And she had to see or speak to another person, not on a screen, at least three times a week.
The first week was hard.
Lucy kept wanting to open her laptop in the evening, and more than once she had to stop herself.
But slowly the rules started to work.
She began to sleep better.
She joined a yoga class on Tuesday evenings, where she made friends with a woman called Priya, who also worked from home.
They started meeting for coffee on Fridays.
She also spoke to Karen honestly about how she had been feeling.
Karen wasn't surprised.
She said that several other designers had been having the same problems.
Together, they agreed that Lucy would come into the agency every Wednesday.
The train journey was still crowded, but now that it was only once a week, Lucy didn't mind it.
She even enjoyed hearing Ben sing again, although she would never tell him that.
Something else happened too.
Her ideas came back.
Walking in the park, sitting in a café or chatting with colleagues gave her the energy she had been missing.
In May, a design she had created for a children's book was chosen by a big publishing company, and Karen sent her a message that said simply: "This is the old Lucy.
Welcome back."
A year after she had first started working from home, Lucy bought a new plant for her office.
This time, she watered it every Monday.
Looking at it, she thought about how much she had learned.
Freedom was wonderful, she realised, but only if you knew how to use it.
If Kate hadn't knocked on her door that Sunday, she might still be sitting in her pyjamas, answering emails at midnight.
Now, at half past five every day, she closes the door of her office, puts on her coat and goes out into the world.

title: The Night Shift
paragraphs: Chloe Bennett had been a nurse for exactly seven months, and tonight was only her fourth night shift in the emergency department of St Mary's Hospital in Leeds.
She arrived at a quarter to eight in the evening, put on her blue uniform and tied her hair back.
Her hands were already a little cold, which always happened when she was nervous.
Before she had started nursing, Chloe used to imagine that hospitals were calm places, where doctors walked slowly along clean corridors.
The emergency department was nothing like that.
It was loud, bright and always full.
People were brought in by ambulance, or they arrived by themselves, holding their arms or their heads.
Some were badly hurt, and others had simply nowhere else to go.
The nurse in charge that night was Maria, a Portuguese woman in her fifties who had been working in the department for over twenty years.
Maria was famous for two things: she never panicked, and she remembered everyone's name.
"Stay close to me tonight," she told Chloe.
"If you're not sure about something, ask.
Nobody will think you're stupid.
It's much worse to guess."
The first few hours were busy but not too difficult.
Chloe cleaned and dressed a cut on a young man's hand, which he had injured while cooking.
She took the blood pressure of an elderly woman who had felt dizzy at the supermarket.
She helped a little girl who had pushed a small plastic toy up her nose.
The girl's father was more frightened than the girl, and Chloe spent ten minutes calming him down.
At around eleven o'clock, a man in his sixties was brought in.
His name was Mr Hughes, and he had been feeling pain in his chest since dinner.
His wife had made him come, although he kept saying it was only indigestion.
Chloe attached him to the heart monitor and took some blood.
Mr Hughes was polite and even made jokes, but Chloe could see that he was scared.
She asked him whether he had ever had heart problems before.
He said no, but that his father had died of a heart attack at the same age.
The doctor, Dr Osei, looked at the results and decided to keep him in for observation.
"He's stable for now," he told Chloe, "but check on him every thirty minutes."
After midnight, the department became much busier.
There had been a car accident on the motorway, and three people were being brought in at the same time.
Maria quickly told everyone where to go.
Chloe was sent to help with a young woman who had broken her leg.
The woman was crying with pain and kept asking about her boyfriend, who had been driving the car.
Chloe held her hand while the doctor gave her something for the pain.
She didn't know where the boyfriend was, but she promised to find out.
For the next two hours, Chloe didn't stop moving.
She carried blood samples to the laboratory, brought blankets, answered phones and wrote notes.
At one point, a drunk man in the waiting room started shouting at the receptionist, and security had to be called.
Chloe had been warned that this happened at night, but it was still frightening to see.
She was so busy that she didn't have time to drink even a glass of water.
At half past two, she suddenly remembered Mr Hughes.
She realised that she hadn't checked on him for almost an hour.
Her stomach went cold.
She ran to his bed.
He was pale and sweating, and he was holding his chest.
"It's getting worse," he whispered.
The numbers on the monitor had changed.
For a second, Chloe couldn't move.
Then she remembered what Maria had told her.
She pressed the emergency button and called for Dr Osei.
Within seconds, the team was there.
Mr Hughes was having a heart attack.
He was given medicine, and the hospital's heart specialist was woken up and called in.
Twenty minutes later, Mr Hughes was taken upstairs for an operation to open the blocked blood vessel in his heart.
When it was all over, Chloe went into the small staff kitchen and sat down.
Her hands were shaking.
She couldn't stop thinking about the hour she had missed.
If she had checked on him earlier, the problem would have been noticed sooner.
If she had come even ten minutes later, he might have died.
Maria found her there a few minutes later.
She made two cups of tea and sat down opposite her.
Chloe told her everything.
She said that she had forgotten about him and that it was her fault.
Maria listened without interrupting.
Then she said, "Chloe, listen to me.
Tonight we had three people from a car accident, a drunk man and a waiting room full of patients.
There were five of us.
You were doing three jobs at once.
Yes, you should have checked on him, and next time you will.
But when you saw that something was wrong, you didn't panic.
You called for help immediately.
That's why he's alive."
She told Chloe that in her first year, she had made mistakes too, and that she still remembered every one of them.
"The day you stop worrying about your patients," she said, "is the day you should stop being a nurse."
At four o'clock, the department went quiet for the first time that night.
Chloe finally had a chance to keep her promise.
She called the other hospital where the young driver had been taken and found out that he only had a broken arm.
When she told the young woman, she started crying again, but this time with relief.
The last hours of the shift passed slowly.
Chloe was so tired that her eyes kept closing.
She drank too much coffee and ate a chocolate bar from the machine, which was the only food she had had since the evening.
Outside, the sky slowly turned from black to grey and then to pale pink.
At half past seven, just before the end of her shift, the phone rang.
It was a nurse from the heart unit upstairs.
She said that Mr Hughes's operation had been successful and that he was awake.
He had asked who the nurse downstairs had been.
He wanted to thank the young woman who had pressed the button.
Chloe went upstairs before she went home.
Mr Hughes was lying in bed with a tube in his arm, and his wife was sitting next to him, holding his hand.
"That's her," he told his wife, smiling weakly.
"That's the one who saved me."
Chloe didn't feel like a hero.
She still felt guilty about the missing hour.
But she smiled and told him to rest.
When she finally walked out of the hospital at eight o'clock, the city was waking up.
People were hurrying to work with coffee and newspapers, and nobody knew what had happened inside the building during the night.
Chloe was more tired than she had ever been in her life.
But as she walked to the bus stop, she realised that she didn't want to do any other job.
Tomorrow night, she would be back.

title: The Inheritance
paragraphs: Tom Harper was twenty-nine and lived in a small rented flat above a noisy café in the city.
He worked in a call centre, where he spent eight hours a day answering complaints about broken washing machines.
He had been doing this job for four years, and he had stopped expecting anything exciting to happen to him.
One Tuesday morning, a thick envelope arrived.
It had been sent by a lawyer called Mr Fletcher, and it was about someone Tom hardly remembered: his great-aunt Edith.
She had died three weeks earlier, at the age of eighty-seven.
Tom read the letter twice before he understood it.
Aunt Edith had left him her house in Ashcombe, a tiny village in the hills, two hundred kilometres away.
Tom phoned his mother immediately.
"Why me?" he asked.
"I only met her once, when I was eight."
His mother was just as surprised.
"She was always a bit unusual," she said.
"She never married, and she didn't like visitors.
Your father used to say that she preferred her bees to people."
A few days later, Tom took the train to meet Mr Fletcher.
The lawyer was a tall, quiet man whose office was full of old books.
He explained that the house was in good condition and that the garden was large.
Then he cleared his throat.
"There is one condition in your aunt's will," he said.
"You may only keep the house if you live in it for a full year.
You must also look after her bees.
If you leave before the year is over, the house will be given to the village, and it will be turned into a library."
Tom laughed nervously.
"Bees?
I don't know anything about bees.
I've never even had a pet."
Mr Fletcher smiled politely.
"Your aunt said you would ask that.
She told me to give you this."
He handed Tom a small notebook with a green cover.
On the first page, in careful handwriting, Edith had written: "Everything you need to know about bees.
Don't be afraid of them.
They can tell when you are."
On the train home, Tom thought about his choices.
If he refused, nothing in his life would change.
If he accepted, he would have to leave his job, his friends and the city.
He made a list of reasons for and against.
The list against was much longer, but he kept thinking about the green notebook.
His best friend, Raj, thought he had gone mad.
"You'll be bored in a week," he said.
"There's no cinema, no gym, probably no internet.
You'll be talking to the bees by Christmas."
"Maybe," Tom replied.
"But I wish I had done something brave before I turned thirty."
In March, Tom handed in his notice and moved to Ashcombe.
The house was made of grey stone, and it had a red door and a garden that went down to a small river.
At the end of the garden stood six white beehives.
On the first night, the silence was so deep that he couldn't sleep.
He kept waiting for the sound of traffic.
The first weeks were hard.
The heating didn't work properly, the nearest supermarket was twenty minutes away by car, and the bees seemed to hate him.
The first time he opened a hive, he was stung three times.
He had forgotten to put on his gloves, even though the notebook had told him to do it.
He sat in the kitchen with ice on his hand and nearly called Raj to say he was coming back.
Then there was a knock at the door.
An old man with a white beard was standing outside with a basket of eggs.
His name was George, and he had been Edith's neighbour for forty years.
"I heard you met the bees," he said with a smile.
"Edith was stung all the time when she started.
She used to say it was the bees' way of saying hello."
George became Tom's first friend in the village.
He showed him how to move slowly near the hives and how to check whether the queen was healthy.
He also told him stories about Edith.
She had been a science teacher in the village school for thirty years.
Every child in Ashcombe had been taught about bees in her garden.
"Half the village learned to read in her kitchen," George said.
"She was strict, but she was kind."
Slowly, Tom began to enjoy his new life.
He found a part-time job at the village shop, where he soon knew everyone by name.
In the evenings he read Edith's notebook and tried to follow her advice.
By summer, the bees no longer frightened him.
He even started to look forward to the mornings when he worked with them.
In July, Tom took his first honey from the hives.
It was dark gold and tasted of flowers.
He put it in small jars and gave one to everyone who had helped him.
Mrs Price from the post office asked if he would sell some at the village market.
Within an hour, all forty jars had been sold.
One rainy afternoon in October, Tom was cleaning the bookshelves in the living room when an envelope fell out of an old dictionary.
His name was written on it.
Inside was a letter from Edith, which had been written two years before she died.
"Dear Tom," it said.
"You probably don't remember me, but I remember you.
When you were eight, your parents brought you here for one afternoon.
Everyone else stayed inside, but you spent two hours in the garden watching the bees.
Before you left, you asked me whether I was ever lonely.
I told you I wasn't, because I had the bees and the village.
You said that when you grew up, you wanted to live in a place like this.
I have never forgotten it."
The letter continued: "I don't know what kind of man you have become.
Perhaps you are very happy in the city.
If so, give the house to the village and don't feel guilty.
But if you have stayed until you found this letter, then perhaps the boy in the garden was right."
Tom read the letter three times.
Then he sat down at the kitchen table and cried for the first time in years.
He didn't remember that afternoon at all, but he knew that she had been right.
In March, exactly one year after he had arrived, Tom visited Mr Fletcher again.
The lawyer asked him if he still wanted to sell the house.
Tom said that he had no intention of selling it.
"I've got bees to look after," he explained.
He did not forget the village, though.
He thought that if Edith had still been alive, she would have liked the idea of a library.
So he turned the large room at the front of the house into a small reading room for children.
Every Saturday, the children of Ashcombe came to borrow books.
Afterwards, wearing white suits that were much too big for them, they followed Tom down the garden to visit the bees.

title: The Film Extra
paragraphs: Lena was a twenty-year-old student who was studying history at university.
Like most students, she never had enough money.
She had been looking for a weekend job for weeks when her flatmate, Chloe, showed her an advertisement online.
A film company was looking for extras for a historical film that was being made in their city.
The pay was eighty pounds for one day, and lunch was included.
"You love history," Chloe said.
"And you might see someone famous.
What have you got to lose?"
Lena sent a photo and filled in a short form.
She didn't expect to hear anything, but two days later she received an email.
She had been chosen to play "a woman at the market" in a scene that was set in 1890.
She was asked to arrive at the film set at six o'clock on Saturday morning.
On Saturday, Lena got up at half past four.
It was still dark when she arrived at an old square in the centre of town.
She hardly recognised it.
The shop signs had been replaced with old wooden ones, the street lights had been covered, and the ground had been covered with straw.
There were horses, carts and more than a hundred people in old-fashioned clothes.
A young woman with a clipboard told her to go to a big white tent.
Inside, Lena was given a long brown dress, a grey shawl and heavy boots that were one size too big.
A make-up artist made her face look tired and dirty.
"Market women worked hard," she explained.
"They didn't look like film stars."
Then someone put a basket of potatoes in her arms.
At seven o'clock, the extras were told to wait in another tent.
Lena sat down next to an older man called Frank, who had been working as an extra for fifteen years.
"Welcome to the film business," he said with a smile.
"Ninety per cent of this job is waiting.
If you've brought a book, you'll be fine."
Lena hadn't brought a book.
She had imagined that filming would be exciting, but nothing happened for hours.
They waited while the lights were moved.
They waited while the cameras were checked.
They waited while it started raining and then stopped.
Frank told her stories about the films he had been in.
He had once been a soldier, a waiter, a passenger on a ship and a dead body.
"The dead body was the best," he said.
"I was lying down for the whole day."
At last, at eleven o'clock, the extras were called to the square.
The assistant director, a man with a loud voice, explained the scene.
A rich young man would ride into the market on a horse, get off and speak to a flower seller.
The extras had to walk around, buy and sell things and look natural.
"And please," he shouted, "don't look at the camera!"
Then everyone became excited, because the main actor arrived.
It was James Morland, who was one of the most famous actors in the country.
Lena had seen all his films.
He was shorter than she had expected, but he had a warm smile.
Between takes, he chatted with the crew and drank tea from a paper cup, just like everyone else.
They filmed the scene again and again.
Each time, Lena had to walk from a fruit stall to the fountain with her basket.
Sometimes the horse moved too early.
Sometimes a plane flew over the square, and they had to stop.
Once, James Morland forgot his words and laughed.
By the ninth take, Lena's feet hurt in the big boots, and her arms ached from carrying the potatoes.
Then it happened.
On the tenth take, just as James Morland was getting off his horse, Lena's boot caught on a stone.
She tripped, and her basket fell.
Potatoes rolled all over the ground, and some of them rolled right under the horse's feet.
The horse moved back nervously.
Lena froze.
She was sure that she had ruined the whole scene.
But James Morland didn't stop acting.
He bent down, picked up a potato and gave it back to her with a little bow.
"I believe this is yours, madam," he said in his character's voice.
Then he helped her pick up the rest, before he walked on to the flower seller as if nothing had happened.
"Cut!" shouted the director.
There was a long silence.
Lena wished the ground would open and swallow her.
She was certain that she would be sent home immediately.
Instead, the director walked over with a big smile.
"That was wonderful," she said.
"It looked completely real.
Can we do it again, exactly the same way?"
Lena couldn't believe it.
She asked whether the director really wanted her to drop the basket on purpose.
The director said that she did.
They filmed the scene four more times, and each time Lena dropped her potatoes and James Morland helped her.
Afterwards, he came over and shook her hand.
He told her that the best moments in films were often accidents.
"If you hadn't tripped, the scene would have been boring," he said.
The rest of the day was quieter.
Lena and the other extras waited again, ate soup and sandwiches in the tent, and walked through a few more scenes in the background.
When they finished at eight o'clock in the evening, she was so tired that she fell asleep on the bus home.
She told Chloe the whole story, but she warned her not to get too excited.
"Lots of scenes are cut from the final film," Frank had explained.
"Don't tell your family until you see it."
Lena followed his advice.
She went back to her studies and almost forgot about the film.
More than a year later, it came out in cinemas.
Lena went to see it with Chloe and a group of friends.
She sat in the dark with her heart beating fast, waiting for the market scene.
When it came, it lasted only twelve seconds.
But there she was, in her brown dress, dropping her potatoes in front of James Morland.
He picked one up, smiled at her and said his line.
The audience laughed warmly.
Chloe grabbed her arm and screamed so loudly that the people in front turned round.
The film was a big success.
In one interview, James Morland was asked about his favourite moment during the filming.
He said that it was the scene with the potatoes, which had not been planned at all.
He explained that a young extra had tripped and that they had decided to keep it.
Lena read the interview five times.
She never became an actress, and she never wanted to.
But she still does extra work sometimes, usually when she needs money for a holiday.
She always brings a thick book, comfortable socks and plenty of patience.
And whenever someone asks her how she can bear the long hours of waiting, she smiles and tells them about the potatoes.

title: The Climate Project
paragraphs: Ms Okafor had been teaching science at Riverside High School for ten years, and she was known for her unusual projects.
One Monday in September, she wrote one word on the board: WASTE.
Then she turned to her class of sixteen-year-olds.
"For the next six weeks, you will work in groups," she said.
"Your task is to find out how much rubbish our school produces and to suggest a way to reduce it.
The best project will be presented to the head teacher."
Most of the class groaned.
Maya Collins, who sat at the back, groaned the loudest.
She had been hoping for something more interesting, like space or robots.
She was put in a group with three other students: Leo, who never stopped talking; Priya, who was very organised; and Sam, who rarely said anything at all.
At their first meeting, nobody knew where to start.
Leo suggested making a poster.
Priya said that a poster wouldn't change anything.
Finally, Sam spoke.
"Why don't we actually count the rubbish?" he asked.
"Then we'll have real numbers."
So for one week, the group stayed after school and went through the school bins.
They wore gloves and old clothes and sorted everything into piles.
It was disgusting work, but the results were shocking.
In just five days, the school had thrown away more than two thousand plastic cups, nine hundred plastic bottles and over sixty kilograms of food from the canteen.
Most of the plastic could have been recycled, but it had all been put in the same bins.
"I didn't realise it was so bad," Maya admitted.
She took photos of everything.
Priya put the numbers into charts, and Leo, who loved talking, offered to present the results.
Their project won easily.
When the head teacher, Mr Barker, saw the photos, he was surprised.
He agreed to their suggestions immediately.
Plastic cups were removed from the canteen, recycling bins were put in every corridor, and students were encouraged to bring their own water bottles.
Within two months, the school's rubbish had been reduced by almost half.
That should have been the end of the story.
But one Saturday, Maya was walking through the town centre when she noticed the bins outside the shopping centre.
They were full of the same things: plastic cups, bottles and takeaway boxes.
She counted the cafés on the main street.
There were fourteen, and every one of them used plastic cups.
On Monday, she told the others what she had seen.
"We changed our school," she said.
"What if we tried to change the town?"
Leo laughed.
"We're sixteen.
Nobody will listen to us."
"If nobody tries, nothing will ever change," Priya replied.
Sam nodded.
In the end, Leo agreed too, mostly because he didn't want to be left out.
Ms Okafor was delighted when they asked for her help.
She explained that the town council made decisions about rubbish and recycling.
Any citizen could present an idea at a council meeting, but they would need strong evidence and public support.
"You'll need to show that people in the town want this," she told them.
For the next three months, the four friends spent almost all their free time on the campaign.
They visited every café on the main street.
They asked the owners whether they would be willing to stop using plastic cups.
Some were interested, but many of them were worried about the cost.
One owner, a grumpy man called Mr Hale, told them to go away and stop wasting his time.
The group didn't give up.
Priya found out that a town in the north had introduced a similar rule two years earlier.
She wrote to their council and asked how it had worked.
The reply was very helpful: the cafés there had actually saved money, because customers who brought their own cups were given a small discount and came back more often.
Meanwhile, Maya made a short video about the waste in their town, which was shared online thousands of times.
Leo, who was finally using his talking skills for something useful, spoke on the local radio.
Sam designed a petition, and they collected signatures outside the supermarket every Saturday morning.
By February, more than three thousand people had signed it.
The council meeting was held on a cold evening in March.
The room was full.
Maya's hands were shaking as she stood up to speak.
She had practised her speech many times, but now she could hardly remember the first sentence.
She looked at her parents in the second row, took a deep breath and began.
She explained what they had found in the school bins and how the school had changed.
She showed the photos of the bins in the town centre.
Priya presented the numbers from the northern town, and Sam handed every council member a copy of the petition.
Then Leo surprised everyone.
He invited a guest to speak: Mr Hale, the grumpy café owner.
Mr Hale stood up slowly.
He admitted that he had been rude to the students at first.
"But they kept coming back," he said.
"In the end, I tried their idea for a month.
My customers liked it, and I spent less money on cups.
I wish I had listened to them earlier."
The councillors asked a lot of questions.
One of them wanted to know who would pay for the new recycling bins.
Another asked whether small businesses would suffer.
The students answered as well as they could.
When they didn't know an answer, they said so honestly and promised to find out.
Two weeks later, Ms Okafor came into the classroom holding a letter.
The council had voted to ban single-use plastic cups in all cafés in the town centre from the following January.
They had also agreed to put recycling bins on every main street.
The rule would be called the Riverside Rule, after the school.
The class cheered.
Leo jumped onto his chair, and even Sam smiled widely.
Maya couldn't stop thinking about the first day of the project, when she had been so bored.
If Ms Okafor hadn't written that word on the board, none of this would have happened.
The rule came into force the next January, and a year later the town's rubbish had been reduced by thirty per cent.
Other towns started asking the students for advice.
Maya, who had once wanted to study robots, decided to study environmental science at university instead.

title: The Wedding Speech
paragraphs: Oliver Grant was thirty-two and worked as an accountant in a quiet office.
He liked numbers because they were clear and honest.
He did not like crowds, parties or speaking in public.
At school, he used to pretend to be ill whenever he had to give a presentation.
Even now, he felt nervous when he had to speak in a meeting with more than five people.
His younger brother, Ben, was the opposite.
Ben was loud, funny and popular, and he made friends wherever he went.
So Oliver was very surprised when Ben came to his flat one evening in January and asked him a question.
"Emma and I are getting married in June," Ben said.
"I want you to be my best man."
Oliver was pleased and honoured.
Then he remembered what the best man had to do.
"Does that mean I have to give a speech?" he asked.
Ben laughed.
"Of course.
That's the best part.
Don't worry, it only needs to be five minutes.
Just tell some funny stories about me."
Oliver said yes, because he couldn't say no to his brother.
But that night he lay awake, imagining a hundred and twenty people staring at him.
He wished Ben had chosen one of his friends instead.
Ben had dozens of friends who would have loved to speak.
For the first two months, Oliver did nothing.
Every time he thought about the speech, he felt sick, so he simply stopped thinking about it.
In April, his mother phoned and asked how the speech was going.
He told her that it was going well.
In fact, he hadn't written a single word.
In May, he finally sat down at his computer.
He searched online for "how to write a best-man speech" and found hundreds of websites.
Most of them recommended starting with a joke.
So Oliver collected jokes.
He found jokes about marriage, jokes about brothers and jokes about wedding cake.
He put them together into a speech and read it aloud to his cat.
The cat left the room.
The next weekend, he practised the speech in front of his friend Nadia, who had been to more weddings than anyone he knew.
When he finished, she was quiet for a moment.
"Well?" Oliver asked nervously.
"The jokes are fine," she said carefully.
"But they could be about anyone.
Where is Ben?
Where are you?
It doesn't sound like you at all."
Oliver knew she was right.
He threw the speech away and started again.
This time, he tried to write funny stories about Ben, as his brother had asked.
But he wasn't good at telling funny stories.
Every story he wrote sounded either boring or unkind.
Two weeks before the wedding, he still had nothing.
He had been working on the speech every evening for a month, and he was exhausted.
He began to imagine terrible things.
What if he forgot everything? What if nobody laughed?
What if he ruined the most important day of his brother's life?
One evening, he visited his parents and went up to his old bedroom to look for some photos.
At the back of a cupboard, he found a box of things from his childhood.
Inside, there was a drawing that Ben had made when he was six.
It showed two boys holding hands.
Under it, in big untidy letters, Ben had written: "My brother Ollie.
He is not scared of the dark when I am."
Oliver sat on the floor and looked at it for a long time.
He remembered the nights when Ben, who had been afraid of the dark, used to climb into his bed.
He remembered teaching Ben to ride a bike and helping him with his maths homework.
He also remembered the year Oliver's first girlfriend had left him, when Ben had driven three hours in the rain to sit with him and watch bad films.
That night, Oliver wrote a completely new speech.
There were no jokes from the internet in it.
He wrote about the two brothers who were so different, and about how they had looked after each other in different ways.
He wrote about the drawing.
Then he wrote about Emma, and about the first time Ben had talked about her.
Ben had said that she was the only person who made him want to be quiet and listen.
The speech took him two hours to write, and it was the easiest thing he had written all year.
On the day of the wedding, the weather was perfect.
The ceremony was held in a small church, and the reception took place in a large hall by a lake.
Oliver managed to enjoy the ceremony.
But during the dinner his hands started shaking, and he couldn't eat anything.
Then the music stopped, and someone handed him a microphone.
A hundred and twenty faces turned towards him.
He stood up, unfolded his paper and looked at it.
For a terrible moment, the words seemed to swim on the page.
His mind went completely empty.
He looked up and saw Ben, who was smiling at him and giving him a small nod.
Oliver put the paper down on the table.
"I should tell you something," he began.
"I'm not very good at speeches.
When Ben asked me to do this, I wanted to run away.
I've been worried about this moment for six months."
People laughed kindly, and he felt a little better.
Then he told them about the drawing.
He took it out of his pocket and held it up.
He told them how his little brother had always believed he was brave, even when he wasn't.
"The truth is that Ben has always been the brave one," he said.
"He talks to strangers, he tries new things, and he isn't afraid to show what he feels.
I've spent my whole life learning from him."
He talked about Emma, and he repeated what Ben had said about her.
He saw Emma wipe her eyes.
Then he raised his glass.
"If someone had told me twenty years ago that this noisy little boy would find someone so perfect for him, I wouldn't have believed it.
To Ben and Emma."
There was a moment of silence.
Then everyone stood up and applauded.
Ben came over and hugged him for a long time.
"You told me you couldn't do speeches," he said quietly.
"That was the best speech I've ever heard."
Later that evening, several guests came to talk to Oliver.
An old aunt told him that she hadn't cried at a wedding for forty years.
A young man asked whether he could copy the idea for his own sister's wedding.
Even Nadia admitted that she had cried.
Oliver still doesn't enjoy speaking in public.
But he learned something important at his brother's wedding.
People don't need you to be perfect or funny.
They need you to be honest.
And Ben's drawing is now in a frame on his living room wall.

title: Ten Years Later
paragraphs: On their last day at school, five friends had sat on the grass behind the sports hall and made a promise.
Whatever happened, they would meet again in exactly ten years, at the same Italian restaurant where they had celebrated their exam results.
Each of them had written their plans for the future on a piece of paper.
The papers had been put in an envelope, and the envelope had been given to Hannah, who was the most organised of them.
Ten years later, Hannah found the envelope in a drawer while she was moving house.
She had almost forgotten about it.
She looked at the date on it and realised that the anniversary was only three weeks away.
That evening, she sent a message to the other four.
She wasn't sure that anyone would come.
To her surprise, everybody replied within a day.
Jack was living in London, Sofia was in Spain, Marcus had stayed in their hometown, and nobody had heard from Ella for years.
Ella was the last to answer, but she wrote: "I wouldn't miss it for anything."
On the evening of the dinner, Hannah arrived first.
The restaurant had been painted and the menus had been changed, but the old owner, Mr Rossi, was still there.
He remembered her immediately.
"The five students who sang so loudly!" he said.
"You were all so young."
Marcus came next.
At school, he had been the quiet one who loved computers.
Now he was wearing a smart jacket and carrying a car key in his hand.
Then Sofia arrived with a big smile and a tan, and Jack came in late, still talking on his phone.
Ella was the last.
Her hair was short now, and she looked tired, but she hugged everyone warmly.
At first, the conversation was a little awkward.
They talked about the weather, the traffic and the food.
But after the first bottle of wine, they began to relax.
They laughed about their old teachers and the time Jack had accidentally set fire to the science lab.
Soon it felt as if they had never been apart.
After dinner, Hannah took out the envelope.
"Do you remember these?" she asked.
Everyone groaned and laughed.
They agreed that each person would read their own paper aloud.
Jack went first.
At eighteen, he had written that he would be a famous musician, living in Los Angeles.
He read it and laughed.
"Well, I do live in a big city," he said.
In fact, he worked in a bank in London.
He had been playing guitar in a band for a few years, but the band had broken up when the other members got married.
"I earn good money," he admitted.
"But I sometimes wish I had tried harder with the music.
If I had moved to America when I was twenty, maybe things would have been different."
Sofia was next.
She had planned to become a doctor, marry at twenty-five and have three children.
Instead, she had left medical school after two years.
"I realised that I hated hospitals," she explained.
She had moved to Spain to learn the language and had never come back.
Now she ran a small hotel by the sea with her partner.
She had no children yet, but she didn't seem to mind.
"My life looks nothing like this paper," she said.
"And I'm glad."
Marcus unfolded his paper and smiled.
He had written that he wanted to leave their town as soon as possible and start his own company.
He had started his own company, but he had never left.
His software business, which had begun in his parents' garage, now employed thirty people.
"I used to think that you had to go somewhere far away to be successful," he said.
"I was wrong.
Everything I needed was here."
Then it was Hannah's turn.
At school, she had always known exactly what she wanted.
She had planned to study law, become a lawyer and buy a house by the age of twenty-eight.
She had done all of those things.
But as she read her paper aloud, her voice became quieter.
"I did everything on the list," she said.
"And last year, I realised that I wasn't happy.
I'd been working twelve hours a day for five years.
I didn't have time for anything else."
She told them that she had recently left her job.
She was moving house because she wanted to start again in a smaller place.
The table went silent.
Then Sofia reached over and squeezed her hand.
"That's the bravest thing anyone has said tonight," she said.
Finally, everyone looked at Ella.
She held her paper for a long time without opening it.
When she spoke, her voice was calm.
She explained that her mother had become seriously ill a year after school.
Ella had given up her place at art college to look after her.
For six years, she had worked in a supermarket and cared for her mother in the evenings.
Her mother had died two years ago.
"I'm sorry we didn't know," Marcus said quietly.
"Why didn't you tell us?"
Ella shrugged.
"Everyone was busy with their new lives.
I didn't want to be the sad friend."
She told them that she had felt embarrassed for years, because she thought she had fallen behind everyone else.
Then she opened her paper.
At eighteen, she had written only one sentence: "I want to make things that make people feel something."
She looked at it and smiled for the first time that evening.
She explained that she had started painting again after her mother's death.
Last month, a small gallery in the city had agreed to show her work.
It would be her first exhibition.
Everyone cheered so loudly that Mr Rossi came out of the kitchen to see what was happening.
When he heard the news, he brought them a bottle of his best wine.
They stayed until the restaurant closed.
Outside, on the pavement, they talked about how strange life was.
None of them had the life that they had planned at eighteen.
Jack wondered aloud whether they would have been happier if everything had gone to plan.
Sofia said that she didn't think so.
"If I had become a doctor, I would never have found my hotel," she said.
Hannah said that she had followed her plan perfectly, and it hadn't made her happy at all.
Before they said goodbye, Ella suggested a new idea.
Instead of writing plans for the next ten years, each of them would write one thing that they had learned.
They wrote them on paper napkins from the restaurant, and Hannah put them in a new envelope.
Three months later, all five of them were standing together in a small gallery, looking at Ella's paintings.
They had already agreed that they would not wait another ten years to meet again.
